articles.title: Russia sends nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
articles.body:
Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
The document said this included the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note said.
The warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, in a commentary on the ministry's website, cited statements by dignitaries from NATO states which she said demonstrated "Russophobia" and a readiness to wage war with Moscow.
These figures, Zakharova wrote, "need to be brought back down to earth. We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed."
"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different sort of war – a very short war."
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded to Russia's message by declaring: "We are a defensive alliance. And stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful."
In its response to the Russian document, seen by Reuters, NATO also said that none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation."
"We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behavior towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," it said.
Asked if the risk of nuclear weapons being used against the Baltics was now real, Rutte told a defense conference in Brussels hosted by broadcaster Euronews: "No, it's not. Putin knows that he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this that seriously."
Risk of miscalculation
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, said it was becoming increasingly hard for Western countries to keep stepping up their support for Ukraine without tipping into direct confrontation with Moscow.
He said the Russian warning may indicate that hardliners are gaining influence in a debate over how to respond to Western actions that include arms supplies to Kyiv, new sanctions on Moscow, interceptions of Russian ships, frequent military exercises and intelligence flights near Kaliningrad.
"They (Russia) expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea - just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war. I see a risk of mutual miscalculation," Sokov said.
In an online interview, he said Russia and Europe were on a collision course. Both sides needed caution and calculation.
Instead of this, the Europeans were applying "full-court pressure," and Russia was delivering a serious warning that this was highly risky, Sokov added.
Europe says it faces 'hybrid war', Russia denies it
In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described these as diplomatic reminders to "hotheads in Europe."
Relations, already dire since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, have sharply worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
A NATO diplomat said: "I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. (It) reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine."
A senior European defense official said: "(This is the) first time since (the) Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious."

articles.title: Zelenskyy visits frontline troops, discusses air defenses with Finnish president
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday that he visited frontline troops in eastern Ukraine and discussed strengthening air defenses with Finnish President Alexander Stubb following Russian strikes.
Zelenskyy said on Telegram that he visited the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade’s command post on the Lyman front in the eastern Donetsk region, presented state awards and discussed the unit’s missions and needs.
He said the brigade, operating alongside other units of the Third Army Corps as part of Operation Vivaldi, had brought more than 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory back under Ukrainian control.
Separately, Zelenskyy said he spoke by phone with Stubb about strengthening defenses following “a new escalation of attacks” against Ukrainian cities and communities.
Ukrainian officials reported at least four deaths in overnight Russian attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported three deaths in the capital, while emergency services said a child was killed in Vyshgorod.
"Almost throughout the entire day, since the night, air raid alerts have continued in Kyiv and other cities and regions, with a constant threat from jet-powered Shaheds. There were also ballistic strikes at night," said Zelenskyy.
The two presidents discussed how best to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses, including F-16 fighter jets and air defense capabilities, according to Zelenskyy.
The attacks have also disrupted economic activity.
Oleksandr Kravchenko, Ukraine’s economy and environment minister, told The Guardian in an interview published Wednesday that missile alerts cost the country an estimated $45 million for every hour they halt business as workers take shelter.

articles.title: Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram bomb while children in grades 1–4 were studying there
articles.body:
The Russian army deliberately struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram aerial bomb while students—children in grades 1–4—were there, Serhii Kryvosheienko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration, reported on 29 September. The strike was one of a series of mass attacks on Ukrainian territory over the past 24 hours.
Across Ukraine, children now begin the school year in bomb shelters, because Russian missiles, drones, and glide bombs keep hitting schools, hospitals, and homes far from the front. The first eight months of 2026 brought more civilian casualties than all of last year, the UN says, and places where children gather are part of that toll.
Kryvosheienko said the Russians aimed the bomb at the school on purpose.
"With no pity or compassion whatsoever, they strike at children? There is nothing human in the enemy! He is not fighting on the battlefield—he is destroying a nation," Kryvosheienko said.
About 40 students were in the school's shelter at the time, a school employee told Suspilne correspondents. Preliminary reports indicate the children were not injured, Suspilne said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the strike on the school.
"Four KABs struck the city center, right at the school building, where classes were underway. Thank you to the teachers and the school administration: the children and teachers were in the shelter, a total of 100 people were evacuated in time," he wrote.
Two people were killed in Sumy, and children are among those injured
Over the past 24 hours, Russian forces carried out more than 60 strikes on 25 population centers in 13 territorial communities of Sumy Oblast, the Sumy Regional Military Administration reported. Two people were killed and 15 others were injured, including two children, according to the administration's figures for each community. Over the course of the day, the oblast was under an air-raid alert for 22 hours and two minutes.
In particular, a 74-year-old man and a 70-year-old woman were killed in the Sumy community as a result of strikes by guided aerial bombs (KABs), the report said. Four people were injured and three people sustained trauma as a result of the Russian attack, including a one-year-old girl. A six-year-old girl was also injured, while a 49-year-old man sustained injuries in a UAV attack.
Over the past 24 hours, the Russians attacked Mykolaiv Oblast with Shahed/Gerbera-type attack UAVs, killing a 56-year-old man, the Mykolaiv Regional State Administration reported. The attack destroyed one detached house, damaged two others and four outbuildings, and caused fires, according to the report.
An 8-year-old girl and an 85-year-old woman suffered acute stress reactions as a result of Russian shelling
Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and 10 population centers in Kharkiv Oblast, according to Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration. Two people were hurt, both with acute stress reactions.
In Kharkiv, an 8-year-old girl suffered an acute stress reaction, as did an 85-year-old woman in the village of Ohurtsivka, Syniehubov reported.
The Russians used various types of weapons against Kharkiv Oblast: one guided aerial bomb (KAB), one multiple rocket launcher system (MLRS), five Molniya-type UAVs, seven FPV drones, and eight UAVs whose type is still being determined, according to the report.
In Kharkiv, Russian shelling damaged the windows of an apartment building, two cars, a private house, and the roof of a shopping center. A car was also damaged in the village of Myronivka, and three cars in the village of Mali Fesky.
The Russians also injured six residents of Donetsk Oblast: three people in Bilbasivka, one person in Sloviansk, one person in Shabelkivka, and one person in Druzhkivka, Donetsk Regional State Administration head Vadym Filashkin reported on his social media.
Over the past day, 18 population centers in Kherson Oblast came under Russian airstrikes, drone attacks, and artillery shelling, leaving five people injured, says Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration. He adds that Russian forces targeted critical and social infrastructure as well as residential areas, damaging two detached houses in particular.
Russian forces carried out 686 strikes on Zaporizhzhia Oblast
Over the past 24 hours, the Russians carried out 686 strikes on 51 population centers in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, but no civilians were injured, co-chair of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council Ivan Fedorov reported, adding that:
- Russian forces carried out 22 airstrikes on 18 population centers.
- 530 UAVs of various modifications, predominantly FPV drones, attacked 37 population centers.
- Five MLRS strikes were recorded against Orikhiv, Novoandriivka, and Kosivtseve.
- 129 artillery strikes hit 19 population centers.
- 44 reports were received concerning damage to infrastructure, homes, and vehicles.
Seven facilities in Zhytomyr Oblast were damaged during the evening and overnight hours leading into 30 September, says Vitalii Bunechko, head of the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration. Food and processing industry enterprises as well as energy facilities came under Russian attack. Four cars also burned as a result of the attack, Bunechko added.
The Russian army attacked three districts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast with UAVs, Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration head Oleksandr Hanzha wrote on social media. The attacks damaged infrastructure, and a fire broke out in one of the communities, he said, adding that there were no casualties.
Air defense forces neutralized three Russian UAVs over Cherkasy Oblast, with no casualties, Ihor Taburets, head of the Cherkasy Regional Military Administration, reported. However, the fall of an enemy target caused a fire at an infrastructure facility, which was quickly extinguished, he added.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukrainian power pylon with steel-cutting drone for 1st time, Zelensky's adviser says
articles.body:
Russia strikes Ukrainian pylon with steel-cutting drone for 1st time, as power outages hit 3 regions
Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
Ukraine's Air Force said that between 6:30 a.m. and 6:30 p.m. local time, Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 254 of 285 drones. Russian forces launched 174 jet-powered drones, 146 of which were intercepted by Ukrainian forces.
As of around 6:30 p.m., 10 drones remained in Ukrainian airspace, the Air Force said.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
Earlier in the morning, the ministry said some consumers in Kyiv and five oblasts had been left without electricity due to Russian strikes, although no nationwide restrictions were initially expected during the day.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.
Ukraine's electricity system was already under strain before the renewed fall attacks.
During the summer, increased demand put additional pressure on the grid during hot weather, while Russian attacks periodically caused temporary outages in different regions. Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned national power grid operator, repeatedly urged consumers to reduce electricity use during peak hours.
Last winter, repeated Russian strikes severely damaged power and heating infrastructure across Ukraine, leaving thousands of homes without heat and power for prolonged periods during freezing temperatures.
Officials have warned that the upcoming winter could be even harsher than the last one. Ukraine has yet to secure funding for its 5.4 billion euro ($6.2 billion) energy resilience plan, according to previous reporting.
The renewed attacks are also coinciding with the first cold spell of the season. Ukraine's State Emergency Service warned that overnight temperatures could fall to between 0 and 3 degrees Celsius (32-37 Fahrenheit) across Ukraine from Oct. 1-3.

articles.title: US imposes sanctions against Russian companies tied to Iran weapons procurement
articles.body:
US imposes sanctions against Russian companies tied to Iran weapons procurement
The United States implemented sanctions on Sept. 29 against several individuals and entities, including two Russian companies, associated with the procurement of Iranian weapons, the Treasury and State departments announced.
The measures target 13 individuals and entities in Russia, Hong Kong, China, and Pakistan as the United States continues to exert economic pressure on Tehran under "Operation Economic Outcast" amid its months-long war with Iran.
Among the Russian entities sanctioned are MG-Flot LLC, whose vessels transport weapons for Russia's Defense Ministry, and Russian aircraft manufacturer JSC Experimental Design Bureau Named After A.S. Yakovlev, according to Reuters.
Previous media reports have found that Russia has supplied Iran with drone components and ammunition in its war with the U.S., and Moscow has also reportedly helped Tehran to target U.S. bases.
Tehran and Moscow have increasingly strengthened relations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In the first year of Russia's war, Iran supplied Russia with Shahed drones to be used extensively against military and civilian targets alike. In return, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept. 1 he would keep supporting Iran and supply it with "necessary goods," as it fights against the U.S. over the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. President Donald Trump attacked Iran in February, a conflict that has continued on and off since then, and severely reduced global oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Amid a tense relationship between Kyiv and Tehran over Iran's support of Russia, Kyiv launched strikes on an Iranian vessel transporting military cargo in the Caspian Sea as recently as July.

articles.title: The Kaliningrad Non-Paper: Decoding Moscow’s Latest Warning to NATO
articles.body:
The unusually direct diplomatic clash between NATO and Moscow over the Kaliningrad exclave marks another escalation in Russia’s effort to use nuclear signaling and hybrid pressure against the Alliance.
By sending a formal “non-paper” to NATO headquarters in Brussels and warning that Russia was prepared to deploy its “entire arsenal” if Alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, Moscow appears to be drawing a deliberately threatening red line around one of its most strategically exposed territories.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska said in August that Russian nuclear rhetoric tends to intensify when Moscow faces setbacks on the battlefield or pressure on its critical infrastructure, arguing that such threats are aimed both at undermining Ukrainian resolve and weakening Western backing for Kyiv.
Nuclear saber-rattling to mask strategic vulnerability
Kaliningrad is one of Russia’s most strategically sensitive outposts.
Wedged between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea and geographically separated from mainland Russia, the exclave sits deep inside a region where NATO has substantially strengthened its military posture since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The accession of Finland and Sweden has further transformed the military geography of northern Europe, giving NATO members control of most of the Baltic coastline and increasing the strategic pressure surrounding Kaliningrad.
Latvia’s Russian Speakers Reject Putin’s ‘Russian World’ as Election Looms
For Moscow, that geography creates an obvious vulnerability. Russia has heavily militarized the exclave, but reinforcing and sustaining it in any serious confrontation with NATO would present major logistical and operational challenges.
The Kremlin’s answer is therefore increasingly asymmetric.
Its warning that Russia could deploy its “entire arsenal” appears designed to push the confrontation into the nuclear realm – raising the perceived costs of even conventional NATO activities around Kaliningrad and attempting to make routine deterrence measures politically harder for allied governments.
NATO has rejected that premise, stressing that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization remains a defensive alliance and that its exercises and deployments do not threaten Russian territory.
The Alliance has nevertheless dramatically reinforced its eastern flank since 2022, including through additional combat-ready forces, air and missile defense, surveillance and new regional defense plans. NATO says those measures are a response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and growing hostile activity against allied states.
The pivot to sub-threshold sabotage
The more important part of NATO’s response may be its linkage of Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric to Russia’s wider campaign of hybrid pressure.
As the conventional war in Ukraine continues, European governments and NATO officials say Russia has increasingly relied on sabotage, cyberattacks, electronic interference, drone incursions and other operations designed to remain below the threshold of open war with the Alliance.
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, has said Russia’s goal is to “break the will” of Ukraine’s allies, urging governments to expose and publicly attribute sabotage and destabilization operations when the evidence allows.
The Baltic region has become one of the most visible theaters for that pressure.
Commercial aviation is already contending with persistent GPS interference across the Baltic, severe enough that Finnair has modified pilot training and operational procedures to account for near-daily disruptions. The interference has intensified alongside Russia’s war against Ukraine and heightened electronic warfare activity in the region.
NATO has separately documented a broader Russian campaign involving sabotage, violence, cyber operations, electronic interference and disinformation across allied territory.
Against that backdrop, Moscow’s nuclear warning over Kaliningrad can be read as another layer of the same strategy: amplify fear at the strategic level while maintaining pressure below the threshold of conventional war.
NATO’s strategy of measured deterrence
NATO’s public acknowledgment of the Russian non-paper and its measured response suggest that the Alliance does not intend to accept Moscow’s framing.
By emphasizing that NATO is defensive and rejecting the threat of force, the Alliance is attempting to deny the Kremlin the argument that its own militarization and nuclear rhetoric are merely reactions to Western aggression.
At the same time, NATO leaders have made clear that Russian intimidation will not produce the outcome Moscow appears to want most: reduced Western support for Ukraine.
Secretary General Mark Rutte has repeatedly argued that Russian hybrid actions should trigger the opposite response, AFP reported.
“Our reaction will always be more support for Ukraine,” he said earlier this month, warning that Moscow’s attempts to create fear and division would not succeed.
Rutte returned to the same point last week, telling allies not to “fall into his trap” by allowing Russian hybrid attacks to distract attention from Ukraine. “Everything he does will lead to more support for Ukraine, not less support for Ukraine,” he said.
The danger, however, remains real.
The concentration of military forces around the Baltic, repeated airspace incidents, sabotage operations, electronic warfare and increasingly explicit nuclear rhetoric all increase the possibility of miscalculation.
Kaliningrad therefore remains one of the most dangerous pressure points in the NATO-Russia confrontation – not necessarily because either side is seeking a direct war, but because Moscow continues to use escalation itself as a political instrument.

articles.title: Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
Air raid alerts warning of Russian attacks cost Ukraine about $45 million an hour, Ukrainian Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko estimated in an interview with The Guardian. He said Ukraine sometimes spends up to 10 hours a day under alerts, which regularly force most businesses in the country to suspend operations while employees take shelter.
To reduce the economic damage, Ukraine’s government introduced a new two-tier alert system: a “red” alert signals the threat of a missile strike and requires people to take shelter, while a “yellow” alert signals a drone threat and allows businesses to keep operating.
More than half of businesses keep operating during “yellow” alerts, Kravchenko said, although the danger remains. On the afternoon of September 28, during a “yellow” alert, a Russian drone struck a building in central Kyiv belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. Two people were killed.
The Kremlin intends to paralyze Kyiv before winter, The Economist reported. Several senior Ukrainian officials told the publication that Vladimir Putin had ordered strikes on civilian sites. One of the officials said, “They want people to be afraid of going to the supermarket.”
Russia did step up its attacks on civilian infrastructure in August and September. Kravchenko sees this as an attempt to “destroy pretty much the entire economy” of Ukraine. He estimated that attacks on factories, warehouses, data centers, and other sites have caused about $10 billion in damage since the start of the year. These losses are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently estimated the shortfall in the 2026 budget at about $27 billion. The figure raised concerns among EU leaders. Kravchenko said spending cuts had reduced the deficit to $20 billion. But Kyiv will need $52.6 billion in external financing next year. Less than half of that amount has been secured so far, and the authorities are discussing further spending cuts and tax increases.
But Kravchenko does not attribute the deficit to mismanagement, corruption, or excessive spending under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. “The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said.
Ukraine now needs to strengthen its air defenses and speed up development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered drones, Kravchenko said. He said Ukraine is better prepared this year for what could be the hardest winter of the war.
The war in photographs: Kyiv and Vyshhorod
Overnight on September 30, Russia attacked Kyiv and the Kyiv region with drones and various types of missiles. Two people were killed in the capital, and four others were injured. In Vyshhorod, in the Kyiv region, a child was killed, and three people were rescued from the rubble of a destroyed house.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia pounds power grid with seven killed in biggest energy attack in months
articles.body:
- 
  Russia has unleashed a widely anticipated air campaign against Ukraine’s energy grid, hitting power facilities and infrastructure around Kyiv and other regions in the heaviest combined attack on energy sites in months. The strikes on Wednesday, in which Ukrainian officials said seven people were killed, came after days of intensifying drone barrages primarily on the capital, a prelude to what many Ukrainians expect to be a winter of attacks intended to plunge cities into cold and darkness while Ukraine is short of air defences. State power grid operator Ukrenergo said it had imposed emergency power cuts as a result of the attack in Kyiv and three surrounding regions – the first time such a measure had been imposed in the capital since the spring.
- 
  “Russia has escalated to massive strikes on energy infrastructure,” the prime minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said on X after the overnight attacks. A child was among the seven dead across Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, with critical infrastructure coming under attack in five regions. Further damage was reported in another five regions, the Ukrainian president added. Forecasters say they expect freezing temperatures at night in Kyiv in coming days.
- 
  Zelenskyy visited a military command post near the town of Lyman near the eastern frontline and praised what he said were gains against Russian forces during a counteroffensive. Ukrainian forces had recaptured 176 sq km (29.3 sq miles) of territory since the start of the operation, he said. “A serious operation, important in many ways for our defence overall and in Donbas in particular,” Zelenskyy wrote, referring to eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, which Russia aims to capture in its entirety. Zelenskyy said the operation had prevented Russian forces from breaking through the rear of defensive lines around Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, part of the network of “fortress cities” Ukrainian forces are defending.
- 
  Ukraine is urging the US to impose sanctions on several Russian entities it says are helping develop Moscow’s Rassvet satellite network as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, its acting ambassador said. Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network and that its goal to start operations in 2027 would pose grave risks to Ukraine. Kyiv planned to issue its own national sanctions against the entities linked to the network, Sienik said, adding: “If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this program possible for Russia and that will be a gamechanger.”
- 
  Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia’s foreign ministry said. Zuppi’s three days of talks coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end the four-and-a-half-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive”. The foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Zuppi also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv’s military used drones last weekend to deliver food and medicine to civilians.

articles.title: Air Force Names 7 to Vie for New MMA Drone Program
articles.body:
The Air Force and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit have narrowed the field to seven companies which will be invited to compete to develop low-cost, semi-autonomous drones to succeed the MQ-9A Reaper, multiple sources confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero all made the cut to continue to develop their candidates for the Massed Modular Aircraft. The companies got the word Sept. 30.
The Air Force and DIU did not immediately respond to queries. Spokespeople from each of the companies either declined to comment or did not respond to queries. It is unclear how many companies submitted proposals, and therefore how many firms were cut from the competition.
An industry source said each company will now submit a proposal to build a prototype MMA.
The Air Force wants to field 500 MMAs by 2032, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
DIU—an acquisition office created to tap into commercial and non-traditional suppliers—sought on July 7 proposals for cheap, attritable drones that could take on the MQ-9’s trademark missions of persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and strike. The Air Force soon confirmed it was working with DIU on the concept.
The solicitation followed the loss of dozens of MQ-9s in operations against Iran earlier this year. DIU said at the time that the military’s reliance on “exquisite” aircraft that cost $30 million or more per tail has become “unsustainable against adversaries utilizing layered defenses enabled by increasingly low-cost antiaircraft capabilities.”
The MQ-9As that were lost did not cost that much, but General Atomics no longer makes that model and instead is offering a larger MQ-9B that can approach or exceed the $30 million level, depending on how it is equipped.
MMA is aiming for a lower price point. DIU’s solicitation sought drones that could fly together in groups large enough to overwhelm an enemy, even if several were shot down, while also forcing the enemy to expend precious anti-aircraft munitions. The Air Force must be able to affordably replace aircraft lost without busting the budget.
Air Force leaders said in a Sept. 3 briefing that they expect to pay about $10 million per MMA airframe, plus whatever sensors or other capabilities are added to it. During that briefing, Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said Secretary Meink pushed to accelerate the MMA fielding schedule in the wake of the Iran losses. Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel, DIU’s military deputy, told reporters that the Pentagon wants to see a prototype within a year of issuing a contract, and field it at scale as soon as 2029.
Responding to the summer solicitation, industry rapidly moved to pitch their concepts. General Atomics pitched a new drone called Wildfire that could carry at least two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, four Joint Strike Missiles, or a similar combination of heavy stand-off weapons.
Swarm Aero, a California startup, proposed a new Group 5 drone dubbed Gamera, and displayed a full-scale model at the Air, Space & Cyber conference.

articles.title: Democratic lawmakers call for protections over third country deportations after ‘indefensible’ court ruling – US politics live
articles.body:
'No beardos, no weirdos, no wimps': Hegseth summons military members for 'State of the Force'
Ariana Baio
The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is providing an update on the US military at his second “State of the Force” address, in Quantico, Virginia, one year after he berated “fat troops” and condemned the military’s “woke” policies.
Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, Hegseth began his announcements by again boasting about his anti-diversity policies.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”
The defense secretary added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth said.
Trump administration airs new taxpayer funded ad celebrating Trump's declaration of war on Iran
The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran.
A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, shows that it features audio taken from Donald Trump’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran.
“This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated.
The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor.
“If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says . “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah”.
As the words “Paid for by the U.S. Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February.
“To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, against a backdrop of dramatic music and images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.”
The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you president Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March.
The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, makes its release now, as the war enters its seven month and continues to alienate Trump’s supporters, baffling.
Judge dismisses Trump administration suit against Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger seeking voter records
A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, over his refusal to hand over unredacted, sensitive voter information to the Department of Justice.
The justice department had demanded that the state’s senior election official email a copy of Georgia’s statewide voter registration list, including each voter’s driver’s license number, social security number and date of birth, arguing that the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law, entitled it to this information.
The US district court judge, Victoria Marie Calvert, ruled that the federal law does not require states to disclose sensitive voter data to the federal government, and does not take precedence over Georgia’s state law protecting the privacy of information provided to the state by registered voters.
Raffensperger was the Georgia state official Donald Trump called on 2 January 2021, in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election, asking him to “find 11,780 votes” for Joe Biden that could be tossed out as fraudulent, which would have allowed Trump to reverse his loss and win the state by one vote.
Trump incorrectly claims pipeline to move liquefied natural gas means 'gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble'
In keeping with his near-constant use of his office for thinly disguised campaign events, Donald Trump had Alaska’s Republican senator Dan Sullivan by his side in the Oval Office on Wednesday when he announced that South Korea plans to spend $54bn to build a liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska.
Sullivan is facing a strong challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola to retain his Senate seat in the November midterm elections.
Unfortunately for Sullivan, the president wrongly suggested that an issue that is infuriating voters in his home state, the high price of gasoline and diesel, would be solved by the pipeline, which will transport an entirely different kind of petroleum, natural gas, when it is completed in three years.
The Alaska LNG project includes an 807-mile (1,299km) pipeline to carry natural gas from the North Slope to a liquefaction facility on Alaska’s southern coast, allowing the fuel to be shipped to Asian markets.
Asked by a reporter about whether there has been any discussion of building another oil pipeline in Alaska, given the high cost of gasoline for consumers, Trump appeared to confuse the liquefied natural gas, known as LNG, with gasoline, which is made from oil.
“Well, this is going to bring those prices down. One of the reasons, Alaska prices are going to come way down,” Trump said of a project that has nothing to do with gasoline used to fuel cars.
After Trump was informed that the the LNG pipeline is going to take three years to complete, which would lower the cost of LNG in Alaska, but have no impact at all on the cost of another petroleum product, gasoline, Trump turned back to reporters and said: “Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble.”
Trump also said that the Korean investment was part of a $200bn package of projects that would also include a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas, another state where his party is in danger of losing a Senate seat.
The announced investment follows pledges South Korea made in 2025 to invest up to $350bn in the US as part of a trade deal in exchange for lower US tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products.
Without providing those details, Trump credited his tariffs for making the announcement possible, saying “our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars.”
“For doing that, I reduced their tariffs to 15%. But they paid to get them reduced,” Trump said. “And, part of that money is going into this project.”
Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
Trump says Netanyahu told him FlyDubai pilot was 'perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job'
Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that he had spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, about the security incident on a FlyDubai commercial flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel on Wednesday.
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job,” Trump said, before giving a dramatic account of the intervention of a passenger who subdued the pilot who reportedly stabbed his co-pilot.
Although witnesses on the flight said that an off-duty pilot then entered the cockpit, pulled the aircraft up and landed in Saudi Arabia, Trump told reporters that “an Israeli plumber” first subdued the attacker, “and this plumber, having never flown a plane, he took the stick, lifted it up, and leveled out the plane before it crashed. Now this is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story I got from Bibi.”
Before we move on from Pete Hegseth’s lengthy address today, it is worth noting that the Pentagon’s in-house “rapid response” social media account, which is dedicated to battling with the media in the style of a political campaign’s opposition research unit, made a point of highlighting the defense secretary’s scathing criticism of the US press corps.
The Pentagon account shared video and a partial transcript of Hegseth addressing reporters he called “the anti-American losers in our media” in prepared remarks that sounded more like a script written by one of Hegseth’s former Fox News producers than a speech by a US cabinet official.
Hegseth went on to say: “The information space is a battle space. Yet our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable. Our media’s shameful lust for political retribution blinds them to the consequences of reckless, so-called ‘reporting’. So-called journalists – juiced up on Trump derangement syndrome – think they’re fighting against our president, but they’re really undermining you – our warfighters.”
“Bottom line: too many of them hate the president more than they love the country. You see, it’s your movement and bases that they reveal to the enemy,” Hegseth told the troops before him. “And ultimately, it’s your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munitions stockpiles.
“All for a banner that will scroll on TV for 30 seconds,” the former Fox weekend host said. “And I know a little bit about banners scrolling on TV for 30 seconds.”
Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military. The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”.
Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment. Nonetheless, the defense secretary slammed the media, and insisted that there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. It’s worth noting that Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand earlier this month.
Throughout his address, Hegseth boasted touted his anti-diversity policies. He insisted that the Pentagon was “no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”
He also announced a new project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”. “Their work will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes,” Hegseth said, noting the project’s findings would be completed and submitted within 120 days, culminating in a full public rollout.
Meanwhile on Capitol Hill, Senate Democrats blocked legislation thatwould allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US. In a 57-43 vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, four Democrats – Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – all broke with their party in support of the bill. However, the legislation failed to achieve the 60 votes needed to advance out of the Republican-controlled upper chamber. More here
Earlier, Democrats in the Senate also blocked legislation that would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and their dependent children from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed along party lines, in a 53-47 vote, failing to clear the 60-vote threshold. Despite widespread support for stopping members of Congress from trading stocks, many Democrats argued the bill didn’t go far enough to actually solve the issue. They also took issue with the fact that the House-passed bill also included a provision which would require photo identification when casting a ballot. More here
Hegseth slams Ivy League universities as 'DEI worshipping woke factories' while announcing new college partnerships
Hegseth’s ‘State of the Force’ address also includes an announcement about partnering with a new group of higher education institutions.
The defense secretary took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges – which the Trump administration has targeted routinely – as “DEI worshipping woke factories”. Hegseth said the department would now partner with other institutions– some of which are known for conservative values, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College.
Other schools joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.
It’s worth remembering that Hegseth attended and graduated from Princeton and Harvard – both Ivy League universities.
Hegseth announces new Pentagon project to 'study warfare' with Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky and Newt Gingrich
The defense secretary announced a new Pentagon project that will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”.

If Palmer Lucky’s name sounds familiar to you, that might be because the Guardian has reported extensively about how his company, Anduril Industries, a major military contractor, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.
The first of six announcements the defense secretary made today was the development of a top-level joint military organization, led by four-star generals, to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities.
“The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” Hegseth said. “The autonomous robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades.”
Per my last post, Hegseth went on to boast about the retention rates in the US military, claiming they are at “record rates” – including “80% of the force on the USS Abraham Lincoln on their historic mission”.
Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment.

The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war.

As we noted earlier, Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military.
The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”.

'No beardos, no weirdos, no wimps': Hegseth summons military members for 'State of the Force'
Ariana Baio
The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is providing an update on the US military at his second “State of the Force” address, in Quantico, Virginia, one year after he berated “fat troops” and condemned the military’s “woke” policies.
Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, Hegseth began his announcements by again boasting about his anti-diversity policies.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”
The defense secretary added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth said.
Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns
Lauren Aratani
An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday.
For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal probe that was dropped in April.
The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation.
“At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said.
Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018m by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027.
The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be nonpartisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail.
Trump latched onto the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features like a VIP dining room and a garden terrace.
In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s.
Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures.
“It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.”
The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said.
During his White House event today, Trump spoke to his need for Republicans to secure the Hispanic and Latino vote in the upcoming midterms.
“I loved you right from the beginning. I loved you for many years before I ever decided to do this political thing,” the president said. “You also know when I build a wall, I’m building a wall to keep bad people out. And you want, and you want those bad people kept out more than anybody.”
This appeal comes after Trump won a record number of Hispanic votes for a Republican president in the 2024 election, but there is concern that the community is now fractured in its support for GOP candidates because of the administration’s immigration crackdown and the cost of living. More than 65% said they are unhappy with the president’s job performance, and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a recent poll from the New York Times/Siena University.
The president falsely claimed that “more oil has come out” of the strait of Hormuz in the past three days than at “any time in history”. While the transport of oil has rebounded in recent weeks, climbing close to prewar levels according to analysts, it has not exceeded that.
The increase in flow through the vital waterway is encouraging, according to those tracking the movement, but it hasn’t yet been reflected in the price. The international benchmark for crude oil still sits just below $100 per barrel.
Trump also welcomed the Pentagon’s news today that the US has finally completed its withdrawal from Iraq.
“This day is a victory for the United States. It’s a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over Isis, which has been completely decimated,” the president said. “I decimated them and took them out in my first administration. So I don’t know what took them so long to be making the announcement that I’m making today.”
Speaking at the White House today to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month, Donald Trump told those attending that they would be among the first to see and walk around the new ballroom when he opens the East Room doors after the event.

articles.title: Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
Ukrinform reports this, citing HUR’s post on Facebook.
The data have been published on the War&Sanctions portal.
“Pantsir” is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range anti-aircraft gun-and-missile systems designed to provide air defense for important areas and individual military and industrial facilities.
Russia also uses these systems to strengthen air defense at low and extremely low altitudes and to protect against mass attacks involving air-launched weapons. Since 2023, the Russians have been installing Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow. This year, another modification of the system, the Pantsir-SMD-E, was spotted there. Unlike earlier variants, it uses smaller TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
Previously, the HUR published information on more than 50 companies involved in producing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-and-missile system.
Now, data on another 23 companies involved in producing 95Ya6 missiles have been disclosed. The 95Ya6 is the main medium-range missile used by various Pantsir modifications.
A key role in developing these missiles is played by the Academician Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau, the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is already known for its involvement in producing weapons for the Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided projectiles and cannons for Su-family fighter aircraft.
At the same time, about one-third of the companies whose information was published today are not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition.
They include:
Komponent plant – a manufacturer of proximity target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles;
Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrotechnical Plant – manufactures and supplies emission and power-supply units for these missiles;
Tambov Elektropribor plant – a manufacturer of steering units for 95Ya6 missiles.
The HUR emphasizes that, to effectively weaken Russia’s military potential, it is important to coordinate restrictions against companies involved in the production of the full range of Russian weapons, rather than offensive systems alone.
Air defense capabilities, including Pantsir systems, protect Russian enterprises that manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as Russian troop formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine and other important facilities in Russia.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the HUR has released data on 14 banks, financial intermediaries and payment systems that enable Russia to conduct international transactions while circumventing sanctions restrictions.

articles.title: Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to make daily life in Kyiv harder before winter, aiming at the ordinary places civilians use rather than at military sites, The Economist reported. Ukrainian officials say the push blends bombing, sabotage, and disinformation, and expect it to peak in November.
Every winter of its full-scale invasion, Russia has tried to freeze Ukrainians into surrender, and each year the strikes reach deeper into ordinary life. The civilian casualties recorded in 2026 have already passed the whole of last year, the UN says.
From the power grid to the grocery store
Russia has already turned its drones on Kyiv's supermarkets, food warehouses, and data centers this year. On 28 September, a Russian jet drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. The strike killed two people, the Academy said. Survivors climbed from the windows of the burning building. A senior Ukrainian official told The Economist the Kremlin now wants shoppers too afraid to enter a store. Russia is also keeping its winter routine, hitting electricity, water, and sewage systems.
Cheaper jet drones that stream live to their pilots
Most of the damage now comes from Russia's cheap jet drones, The Economist said. Pilots guide them onto targets and watch a live video feed. They are hard to stop, and Russia's ballistic missiles are deadlier still as Ukraine's supply of Patriot interceptors dwindles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had agreed a new Patriot interceptor package, but it remains short of interceptors of its own. A security official told The Economist that Russia has thousands of drones stockpiled and plans to use its entire ballistic missile stock within two months.
War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages
Sabotage, chaos, and a city that won't switch off
Ukraine's counter-intelligence services say they foil seven or eight Russian plots a week, and officials believe some sleeper cells remain. The campaign's third element, disinformation, targets war fatigue and corruption scandals. Russia runs the same plan every year, hoping its bot farms will push Ukrainians onto the streets to demand surrender, said Andrii Kovalenko, who heads the Center for Countering Disinformation at the National Security and Defense Council.
"It's nonsense," he told The Economist, adding that someone is feeding the idea to Putin so they can steal more money.
Kyiv is also far harder to shut down than Moscow assumes, Kovalenko said. The city's internet is too decentralized for a handful of strikes to knock out, The Economist noted. Energy expert Olha Babii said the test is how fast crews restore power, not whether it can be destroyed. The capital is emptying, its population down from about 3.7 million to 3.3 million by The Economist's count.

articles.title: The Prime Minister of Bulgaria called on the EU to engage more actively in dialogue with russia and criticized arms supplies to Kyiv
articles.body:
The Prime Minister of Bulgaria called on the EU to engage more actively in dialogue with russia and criticized arms supplies to Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
Rumen Radev called on the EU to intensify diplomatic dialogue with russia in order to end the war and reduce the nuclear risk. He criticized arms supplies to Ukraine.
The European Union should become more actively involved in diplomatic dialogue with Russia in order to end the war in Ukraine and prevent a devastating nuclear strike. This was stated by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, reports UNN, citing Euronews.
Details
He also criticized the continued supply of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine, calling it an unsuccessful strategy of "peace through strength."
There is a limit to simply transferring weapons and providing support, because the ultimate architecture of the world will be shaped by diplomacy, not by arms supplies. Therefore, we call for listening to one another more closely and opening channels of communication. The problem is that no one is raising the issue of the nuclear risk. Does it exist? Perhaps not, I do not know, but it is a risk
He recalled a statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who said that a war between Russia and Europe would be "quite different" and "very short." Radev criticized "this manner of speaking" by the Kremlin, but called on European leaders to consider what further escalation could lead to.
"There is a nuclear trump card. We must take this into account. We cannot turn a blind eye to the fact that there are nuclear weapons on our continent and that nuclear warheads are held in Russia's arsenal. And this is part of the calculation in this game," the Bulgarian prime minister concluded.
We remind you
In September, another ammunition depot exploded in Bulgaria; previously, facilities belonging to this company had been linked to attacks by Russian agents.

articles.title: Russia threatens NATO with a nuclear strike if the alliance tries to blockade Kaliningrad
articles.body:
Russia threatens NATO with a nuclear strike if the alliance tries to blockade Kaliningrad
Russia’s embassy in Ireland posted a nuclear warning on social media, citing unspecified “reports coming in” about NATO preparations for an air and naval blockade of the Kaliningrad region:
There should be no mistake – Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate [the] Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.
Russia “has no plans to escalate tensions with Europe,” the embassy said, while “Europe’s irresponsible and shortsighted political elite is playing a dangerous game.”
The same warning appears in a document Russia sent to NATO and Reuters obtained. In it, Moscow accuses the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries “a high risk of direct armed conflict.”
In its written response, NATO said none of the alliance’s exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. “We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behavior towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” it said, according to Reuters.
The embassy’s post responded to statements by European politicians about an increase in Russian hybrid attacks against Ukraine’s allies.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. articles.title: “We have no legal obstacles” – Rinkēvičs on deploying nuclear weapons in Latvia
articles.body:
Earlier this month, the Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, backed in a first vote the removal of a constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons in the country. Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory.
Rinkēvičs stressed that Latvia’s Constitution contains no such prohibition.
“We have no legally established obstacles in our laws to the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia,” the President said.
He explained that in 2003, as Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member state had affirmed that it would impose no restrictions on the implementation of NATO’s full collective security mechanism, including participation in the Alliance’s nuclear deterrence system.
“If such a need arises and if NATO makes such a collective decision, nuclear weapons will be deployed in Latvia,”
Rinkēvičs said.
At the same time, he stressed that there are currently no specific discussions about deploying nuclear weapons in Latvia.
Commenting on the United Kingdom’s offer to extend nuclear protection to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) – the Baltic states, Nordic countries and the Netherlands – Rinkēvičs argued that without nuclear deterrence, several conventional wars would likely have spread across Europe long ago.
The use of nuclear weapons is an absolute last resort, but their existence deters an aggressor from unpredictable or large-scale actions, Rinkēvičs said.
The President noted that the United Kingdom is already part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence system and that Latvia is already protected by NATO’s nuclear umbrella, provided by the United States and the United Kingdom. As a JEF member, Latvia views all additional security measures and arrangements positively.
“We understand that this remains part of NATO’s overall policy,”
the President said.
As previously reported, the United Kingdom’s offer was confirmed by the head of the Royal Navy, General Gwyn Jenkins, during a visit to Finland on Monday, where he met Heikki Autto, chairman of the Finnish parliament’s Defence Committee.
“The [British] head of the armed forces has emphasised the United Kingdom’s strong commitment to JEF cooperation, and these new opportunities have also been created through that cooperation,” Autto told Finnish news agency STT, commenting on his meeting with Jenkins.
“Finland will be under the nuclear umbrella, and this will be guaranteed by submarines currently patrolling the Atlantic Ocean,” Jenkins confirmed.
An agreement on the creation of a new type of combat force within the JEF is expected to be signed in November.
The new group will have wartime defence plans and is expected to be capable of immediately engaging in military operations in the event of a threat from Russia.
The JEF is a coalition of ten like-minded countries – Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom – comprising high-readiness forces capable of responding rapidly to crises in the High North and Northern Europe.
The coalition was established in 2014 at the initiative of the United Kingdom in response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Finland and Sweden joined the JEF in 2017, before becoming NATO members.

articles.title: ‘There is no immediate threat to NATO territory,’ NATO’s Rutte tells Euronews
articles.body:
NATO chief Mark Rutte told Euronews there is no immediate threat to the alliance and he does not take Russia's Kaliningrad nuclear warning seriously, saying Moscow is trying to distract from its struggles in Ukraine.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has told Euronews there is no immediate threat to the alliance's territory, adding that he does not take Russia's nuclear threats seriously because Moscow could never win a confrontation with NATO.
"We have prepared for this, we have planned for this, and this is true for the whole of NATO," Rutte said at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels on Wednesday.
"We will defend every inch of NATO territory. That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it."
His remarks follow media reports that Russia sent NATO a letter warning it against any attempt to cut off the exclave of Kaliningrad from the Russian mainland. Moscow said it was ready to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons.
"We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine," Rutte said.
Rutte declined to confirm the contents of the letter, saying it was up to Russia to disclose them. He dismissed the idea of a concrete nuclear threat or escalation against the Baltic states.
"Everybody knows that he [Russian President Vladimir Putin] can never win against NATO. I don't take this seriously. But of course, we have to reply and make clear that NATO is a defensive alliance, as I said, and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats," he said.
The NATO chief said Russia is losing 43,000 troops killed or seriously wounded a month on the front line. He added that Kyiv is doing much better than a year ago and that allies continue to provide military support.
For Rutte, NATO should stay calm, keep backing Ukraine and ramp up its defence investment.
"If necessary, of course we will defend ourselves. But the most important thing is this is all happening because the war is not going well for him in Ukraine. He wants to divide us. He wants us to lose attention when it comes to Ukraine," Rutte said.
