articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine are likely about to get worse, analyst says
articles.body:
Russia is stockpiling weapons to intensify attacks on Ukraine, analysts say
Kyiv — A daytime Russian attack on Ukraine Monday damaged civilian buildings and wounded more than 100 people across the country, according to local authorities.
A drone exploded into the National Academy of Sciences in the heart of Kyiv. Hours later, a second drone damaged a private medical clinic just blocks away. In Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, emergency crews rushed to evacuate wounded civilians from a business center also hit in broad daylight.
And yet, the attack could have been much worse.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia used 124 attack drones from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Monday — much fewer than in previous barrages this year, which have regularly included more than 500 drones and 50 missiles within the same time frame.
Analysts and Ukrainian officials told CBS News that Russia is stockpiling weapons so that it can launch intensified late-autumn and winter barrages.
During Monday's attack, Russia used primarily "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept. Ukraine's Air Force said that 86 of the 124 drones used in the attack were jet-powered.
Since Russia began deploying the new models in June, Ukraine's interception rate against them is 57% — a sharp drop-off from the military's 90% to 95% success in intercepting older models.
Russia has two models of jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, and has been stockpiling both. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, estimates that Russia will produce 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 in September, and projects those numbers to grow each month.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has used just 7,700 jet-powered drones in attacks so far this year.
Viktoriia Chekalina, an analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center, estimates that Russia has stockpiled 450 to 700 units of the older non-jet-powered drones, the newer jet-powered models and dummy, non-explosive drones known as "Banderols" during each Russian attack this spring and summer.
"Despite the capacity to launch 600-1,000 units in a single massive attack, only about 150-300 drones were actually used," Chekalina told CBS News, explaining that attacks this autumn and winter "could reach around 1,500 units per one raid."
Because Russia has found success striking targets with relatively small barrages of jet-powered drones, it has also managed to save up its cruise and ballistic missiles, which are vastly more expensive and difficult to manufacture.
In the early spring and summer, Russia's attacks on Kyiv included barrages of over 70 cruise and ballistic missiles multiple times per month, according to estimates released by Ukraine's Air Force. In August, Ukraine stopped publicly releasing the numbers of missiles Russia used in each attack, but military analysts told CBS News that there was a drop-off in the number of mass-missile barrages in August and September.
Over this period, Russia has also increased its production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Chekalina said Russia has surpassed its missile production targets by 110% to 120% and estimated that it had stockpiled 130 ballistic missiles by August.
Solutions to countering Russia's ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones remain elusive. Ukraine continues to run dangerously low on American-made PAC-3 ballistic interceptors. And in an address this week, Zelenskyy said that while new defenses against jet-powered drones are being tested, they are not yet ready to be scaled, raising concerns that Ukraine may remain vulnerable heading into winter.
"Russia's goal during winter campaign will be complex: they will focus on attacking electrical and heating infrastructure as they are critical for civilians," Chekalina said. "At the same time, they will use turbojet drones along with missiles on local businesses, warehouses, and other targets."

articles.title: Moscow issues warning to NATO over Russian exclave
articles.body:
Moscow issues warning to NATO over Russian exclave
Increased NATO military exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region and aggressive rhetoric from members of the US-led bloc are raising the risk of a direct armed conflict, Moscow has warned.
Russia has sent NATO a warning stressing its determination to protect the Russian exclave in the Baltic region “with its entire available arsenal,” according to a statement published on Monday by the Russian Embassy in Belgium, which hosts the bloc’s headquarters.
The message alluded to remarks made earlier this month by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who said there are “hardly any troops” in Kaliningrad Region and urged NATO to increase its military posture near Russia’s borders so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed receiving the Russian message and accused Moscow of irresponsible rhetoric.
”We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said.
Western officials have frequently described Russian statements invoking its nuclear deterrent as “blackmail,” while presenting NATO’s own nuclear-sharing arrangements as a pillar of collective defense.
France has offered to discuss the possible deployment of its nuclear weapons in other European NATO countries, arguing that this could reduce the bloc’s dependence on the US. Under NATO’s existing nuclear-sharing arrangements, American nuclear bombs are stored in several European countries, while personnel from non-nuclear member states train for missions involving their potential use.
Russia has repeatedly rejected Western claims that it intends to attack NATO before the end of the decade, describing such warnings as warmongering aimed at persuading voters to support sharply higher military spending.
Moscow, in turn, views NATO’s military preparations as potentially paving the way for an attack on Russia. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has repeatedly warned that any such conflict would be extremely brief, implying that Moscow could resort to nuclear weapons.
The Russian Embassy in Ireland used more direct language, saying on Tuesday that Moscow is prepared to use nuclear weapons in response to an attempted NATO blockade of Kaliningrad Region and may consider pre-emptive military action in such a crisis.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday it was “natural for our diplomats to try and remind hotheads in Europe about our doctrinal documents,” in response to the rhetoric coming from Poland and other nations.

articles.title: Russia just accidentally crashed its first Tu-95 bomber in 11 years. Its missiles will keep striking Ukraine anyway
articles.body:
- A Russian Tu-95 bomber crashed on takeoff in Russia's Far East on Tuesday, the type's first crash in 11 years
- It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 the Russians have lost in the current wider war, and they can't build more
- But Russia still has enough bombers to keep up its missile raids on Ukraine
A Russian air force Tupolev Tu-95 Bear bomber crashed on takeoff, apparently from Ukrainka air base in Amur Oblast in Russia's Far East. The Russian defense ministry said the plane was on a training flight without munitions and blamed a technical fault. The crash, while reportedly accidental, is still a win of sorts for Ukraine. Every bomber the Russians lose is a bomber they can't immediately replace—and sortie for missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.
The problem for Ukraine is that Russia still has bombers to spare. It'll take more than a few crashes or drone raids on Russian bomber bases to cut into Russia's capacity to bombard Ukraine.
That's why Ukraine needs missile-armed fighters, ground-based self-propelled guns, speedy interceptor drones, and long-range surface-to-air missiles such as American-made Patriots, among other air defenses. The Ukrainians can't prevent missile attacks by destroying bombers or waiting for bombers to crash; they need to shoot down missiles as they near their targets.
A security camera on the ground recorded a large aircraft plunging toward the ground in Amur Oblast on Tuesday night. Video from the crash site confirmed it was one of the Russians' four-engine, propeller-driven Tu-95s, aging workhorses in Russia's escalating campaign of missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The crash killed six crew and left one survivor injured, according to Russian state media. It is the first Tu-95 to go down in 11 years, Defense Express notes, and the first known non-combat loss of the type since the full-scale invasion.
It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 Russia has lost since widening its war on Ukraine in February 2022. Ukrainian drones caught two Bears on the ground at Engels-2 air base in Saratov Oblast in July and August. On 1 June 2025, Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb—coordinated strikes on Russian bomber bases by more than 100 small drones smuggled across Russia in trucks—destroyed as many as four Bears at Olenya air base on the Kola Peninsula and another four at Belaya air base in Irkutsk Oblast.
Now the Russian air force may be down to somewhere between 36 and 44 working Tu-95s, depending on the count, the youngest of which rolled out of the factory in the 1990s. That matters because the Tu-95 is, like the jet-propelled Tupolev Tu-22M bomber, out of production. Vendors have gone out of business. The skilled workers who assembled the types retired decades ago.
While the Russians can still build one or two Tupolev Tu-160 jet bombers every year, slowly growing a fleet that currently stands at around 18 active planes, that's far too few new bombers to replace combat losses as the wider war grinds through its 56th month.
Slow attrition
The Russians have also lost at least nine Tu-22Ms, and possibly far more: Defense Express estimates losses at up to 70% of the combat-ready fleet since 2022. All told, Russia's bomber force has shrunk to around 105 planes since the wider war began, or fewer.
Equally problematically for the Russians, the old Tu-95s and Tu-22Ms that carry out the majority of air-launched cruise missile strikes on Ukraine are wearing out from heavy use; not all are available for front-line use as more airframes spend more time in deep maintenance.
Ukraine is working down the short list of ships that shell its cities with cruise missiles. A Neptune reached one of them tied up at its own pier
But a Tu-95 carries as many as eight Kh-101 cruise missiles at a time; a Tu-22M carries up to three Kh-22s or Kh-32s. A Russian drone and missile strike might include just a dozen or so air-launched cruise missiles launched by a handful of bombers. A raid on 8 September involved just four Tu-95s and two Tu-160s.
The Russians don't need 105 bombers to sustain six-bomber raids once or twice a week, even as those bombers suffer more and more wear and tear. Ukraine would have to take out a lot more Russian bombers, and fast, to put a dent in Russian strikes.
Unless and until that unlikelihood happens, Ukraine will still need to defeat Russian raids inside Ukraine—by shooting down hundreds of incoming drones and missiles at a time. But that's getting harder as the Russians deploy faster jet-propelled Geran drones and more ground-launched Iskander missiles, combining them with the bomber-launched missiles in complex packages that routinely overwhelm ammunition-starved Ukrainian air defenses.

The US imposed sanctions on 13 individuals and entities accused of helping Iran procure weapons and military components, Reuters reported on September 29.
The measures targeted people and companies based in Iran, Russia, China, Hong Kong, and Pakistan. Reuters wrote that the sanctions are part of the US President Donald Trump administration’s effort to economically isolate Tehran and pressure it to negotiate an end to the war that began with a US-Israeli strike on Iran on February 28.

“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated.
The Treasury Department described the measures as an attempt to hinder Iran’s ability to rebuild its weapons programs and raise the costs for foreign companies and individuals supporting its procurement networks, Reuters noted.

articles.title: If NATO collectively decides to do so and there is a need, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia - Rinkevics  - The Baltic Times
articles.body:
RIGA - If NATO collectively decides and there is a need to do so, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics told members of the press today.
The Lithuanian Seimas voted this month in a first reading to support the repeal of the constitutional ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory. Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction or foreign military bases may not be located on Lithuanian territory.
Rinkevics emphasized that the Latvian Constitution does not contain such a ban. "We have no legally established obstacles in our laws to the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia," said the president.
He explained that in 2003, as Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member state had confirmed that it would not impose any restrictions on the full implementation of NATO’s collective security mechanisms, including participation in the nuclear deterrence system. "If the need arises and if such a collective NATO decision is made, nuclear weapons will be deployed in Latvia," Rinkevics stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that no specific negotiations regarding the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently underway.
Commenting on the United Kingdom’s offer of nuclear umbrella to the member states of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF)-the Baltic states, the Nordic countries, and the Netherlands- Rinkevics argued that without nuclear deterrence, several conventional wars would have long since broken out in Europe. The use of nuclear weapons is a last resort, but they deter aggressors from unpredictable or large-scale actions, Rinkevics noted.
The politician pointed out that the United Kingdom is already part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence system and that Latvia is currently under the NATO nuclear umbrella provided by the United States and the United Kingdom, but as a member of JEF, Latvia views all additional security measures and elements positively. "We understand that this is still part of NATO’s overall policy," the president said.
As reported, the United Kingdom has offered a "nuclear umbrella" to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) military partnership (the Baltic states, Nordics countries and the Netherlands) as part of a wider defence agreement.
The umbrella is a security guarantee by a nuclear-armed state to protect a non-nuclear ally.
The offer was confirmed during a visit by General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the UK’s Naval Staff, to Finland on Monday, where he met with MP Heikki Autto (NCP), chair of parliament’s defence committee.
It is believed that the JEF member countries will sign an agreement at a meeting in Oslo in November.
The deal would mean a separate nuclear umbrella outside of Nato’s extended deterrence strategy offered by the US, UK and France to all non-nuclear member states within the alliance.
"Finland is under the nuclear umbrella. It is guaranteed by our submarines, which are patrolling the Atlantic right now," Jenkins said.
JEF is a coalition of ten like-minded countries-Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, the United Kingdom, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, and Sweden - that comprises high-readiness forces capable of responding rapidly to crises in the high north and Northern Europe.
The coalition was established in 2014 on the initiative of the United Kingdom in response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Finland and Sweden joined the JEF in 2017, even before these countries were admitted to NATO. The JEF is now considered a first-response force that complements NATO.

articles.title: Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic

Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
BRUSSELS – Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a “dangerous and reckless course” that entailed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”.
The document said this included the possibility “of Russian strikes against decision-making centres in the alliance’s member states right from the outset of the conflict”.
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” said the text, classed as a “non-paper” – diplomatic jargon for an informal document.
In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Russia also rejected Western allegations that it poses a threat to Europe.
The statements said Russia had no intention of attacking NATO countries but warned that any aggression against Kaliningrad – a heavily militarised Russian territory that is sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania – would be met with the strongest possible response.
The warnings highlight a sharp rise in tension between Russia and European countries, which accuse Moscow of stepping up a “hybrid war” on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
NATO slams ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’
NATO spokeswoman Allison Hart confirmed Russia had sent a non-paper to the alliance but did not disclose its contents.
“We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia. We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine,” she said.
A senior European defence official said: “(This is the) first time since (the) Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious.”
A NATO diplomat said: “I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. (It) reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine.” REUTERS

articles.title: 'We will defend every inch of NATO territory’: Rutte dismisses Russia’s nuclear threat
articles.body:
Aysu Bicer
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Wednesday dismissed Russian nuclear warnings over Kaliningrad, saying Moscow could not win a confrontation with the alliance.
Speaking at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, Rutte said NATO was prepared to defend its territory.
“We will defend every inch of NATO territory. That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he said.
His comments followed reports that Russia, in a letter, had warned NATO against any attempt to cut off Kaliningrad, its western exclave between Poland and Lithuania, saying it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons.
Rutte declined to confirm the contents of the reported letter but rejected the suggestion of an imminent nuclear threat to the Baltic states.
“We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said.
Rutte also said Russian President Vladimir Putin could not defeat NATO. “Everybody knows that he can never win against NATO. I don't take this seriously.”
 
Europe’s defense role
Rutte said Russia was suffering heavy losses in Ukraine and claimed 43,000 troops were being killed or seriously wounded each month.
He said Moscow was trying to divide NATO allies and shift attention away from the battlefield.
“If necessary, of course we will defend ourselves. But the most important thing is this is all happening because the war is not going well for him in Ukraine. He wants to divide us. He wants us to lose attention when it comes to Ukraine,” Rutte said.
The NATO secretary general also said Europe must become more capable of handling security threats without relying so heavily on Washington.
“Why are the Americans doing it, taking out the Iranian nuclear capability? Because we can't. But in the future, we have to make sure that as Europeans, we can do this ourselves,” he said.
Rutte said increased European defense spending should eventually allow the continent to assume greater responsibility while keeping the US engaged in NATO.
“Still, the US being involved not only in the nuclear sense but also in the conventional sense, but the Europeans taking much, much more responsibility for the defense of this part of NATO,” he said.

articles.title: Fire Point uses data from strikes by Russian Iskander missiles and North Korean missiles in the development of Freyja
articles.body:
Fire Point uses data from strikes by Russian Iskander missiles and North Korean missiles in the development of Freyja
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point is integrating data on strikes by Iskander and North Korean missiles into Freyja's algorithms. The first interception is planned by mid-2027.
The Ukrainian defense company Fire Point collects and analyzes data on Russian strikes using Iskander ballistic missiles and North Korean missiles in order to integrate the information obtained into the algorithms of the European Freyja anti-ballistic system. Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said this during her speech at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit 2026 in Brussels, UNN reports.
When is the interception of ballistic missiles planned?
We are stockpiling interceptor missiles for the future, conducting trials and system integration, and testing it in real combat conditions in Ukraine. We are also collecting all the data from attacks against us involving Iskanders and North Korean missiles and incorporating it into Freyja’s algorithms
The company expects to receive some of the improvements to the system’s MVP (minimum viable product, or first working version) by the end of 2026.
Our goal is to conduct a "zero" test this year, and achieve an actual interception by the middle of next year—and that is an extremely ambitious goal. To achieve it, everyone must work in exceptionally close coordination. There must be no delays in supplying radars, issuing licenses, or signing individual documents
Iryna Terekh explained that the developers had compressed the process of creating an anti-ballistic program from 40 years to slightly more than two years. According to her, the project is currently undergoing an intensive phase of technical integration and testing.
But it is still shots and launches, launches and launches, until we achieve a result
What is special about Freyja?
The Fire Point CEO recalled that Freyja is being developed as an anti-ballistic system to protect Europe, and that its concept takes into account the experience of the war in Ukraine, including the scale and number of missile threats.
She noted that initially Freyja would not be able to replace the American Patriot air defense system, which remains one of the best systems in the world. However, Patriots were not designed to handle the number of threats Ukraine is facing.
That is why every element of Freyja is designed according to the design-for-manufacturing principle. In other words, from the outset, the system is intended to be scalable, relatively inexpensive, reproducible, and as independent as possible from critical external components or technologies.
In particular, Fire Point is working to create a system using European components, which will allow Freyja to be independent of U.S. ITAR export controls and Chinese components.
The company places primary emphasis on system interoperability and avoiding dependence on a single manufacturer.
An open architecture makes it possible to combine solutions from different European manufacturers into a single system. This means more alternatives, less dependence on individual suppliers, and the ability to quickly integrate new technologies
No less important is the absence of the so-called kill switch—a "switch" that could deprive the owner of an air defense system of the ability to use it. In other words, using Freyja will not require permission from partners or the manufacturer.
If you own your air defense system, you must truly own it
How many interceptors will be produced per year?
As already noted, Fire Point is currently working on stockpiling FP-7.x interceptor missiles for Freyja and scaling up their production. The company plans to apply to Freyja the approach it has already used when scaling up its other developments.
Regarding interceptor missiles, it should be understood that 600–700 interceptors per year will not change anything. We live in a world where the threat will only grow, and the count must be in the thousands and thousands of missiles
The company took this into account when developing the FP-7.x.
The FP-7X interceptor missile from Fire Point, which is currently part of Freyja, was designed for a production capacity of at least several thousand units per year. Of course, much work remains ahead to make this a reality, but it is possible because the missile was designed for future scaling from the very beginning
What is Freyja?
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Zelenskyy discusses Ukraine's air defense, F-16 needs with Norwegian PM
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed Ukraine's needs regarding air defense and the provision of F-16 fighter jets to counter Russian escalation with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Jonas Gahr Støre.
“We discussed what Ukraine needs to defend against this savage escalation, first and foremost air defense and support for our F-16s. We are coordinating our steps and working to provide greater protection for people’s lives and security,” Zelenskyy said on X Wednesday.
According to him, 24 people have been wounded and seven killed, including a child, in Russian strikes on Ukraine since the start of the day alone.
He also briefed Støre on the relentless Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks.
“We are coordinating our steps and working to provide greater protection for people’s lives and security. I thank the Prime Minister personally, as well as all of Norway, for the unwavering support,” the President added.

articles.title: 189 combat engagements at front in past day, heaviest fighting in Kostiantynivka direction – General Staff

articles.title: US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
articles.body:
US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
September 30, 2026
After more than ten years, US forces are to withdraw from their remaining military bases in Iraq on Wednesday.
"Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests," the Pentagon said in a statement.
The Pentagon added that it will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
"This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
“It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship,” he said.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that October 1, the day following the coalition's departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.
It is "a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq's path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions," the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.
The troops were deployed in Iraq and Syria in 2014, to tackle the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group, which had taken over large swathes of both countries.
The IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.
The complete departure of US troops from Iraq comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, triggering widespread upheaval and chaos, before the rise of IS.
Iran celebrates US withdrawal from Iraq
Iran and its allies celebrated the withdrawal of US forces, which was agreed upon in 2024 by then-US President Joe Biden. The agreement has now been executed under Donald Trump's term even as US continues to wage a war against Iran.
Iran, which wants a US-free Middle East, sees the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal of the US troops from Iraq has raised threats of diminished security in the region as Iran-backed Shi'ite militias are vying to gain more control and potentially regroup 'IS'.
US withdrawal leaves Kurds in Iraq anxious
The withdrawal leaves the the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, where most of remaining US bases operated, vulnerable.
Kurds in Erbil, capital of the Kurdistan region, told AFP news agency they are increasingly anxious about their safety from drones that have repeatedly targeted their autonomous canton, once the US air defense systems are removed.
“The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said in a statement.
Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

articles.title: Ukraine’s President Zelensky thanks Belgium for the delivery of three F-16 fighter-jets by the end of the year
articles.body:
By the end of the year, Belgium will deliver three F-16 fighter-jets to Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted plans of the delivery on social media site X. He intends to use an accelerated procedure to make this possible.
Ukraine’s President Zelensky thanks Belgium for delivery of three F-16 fighter-jets by the end of the year
The planned delivery of the three F-16 fighter jets was announced earlier this year by Defence Minister Theo Francken (Flemish nationalist N-VA), both in the Belgian parliament and on the sidelines of President Zelensky’s visit to Brussels.
In total, Belgium is supplying seven F-16 fighter-jets to Ukraine this year: four of them have already been handed over to the Ukrainians but are de facto still at Sabca in Gosselies. At the aerospace company, the aircraft are being used to train Ukrainian technicians to work on them.
These aircraft are too old to fly and can, at best, only be used for spare parts.
The three aircraft that Belgium will deliver by the end of the year can, however, still be used, explains VRT NEWS defence specialist Jens Franssen.
“They have nearly 8,000 flying hours on the clock, which means they are virtually no longer airworthy here.” However, they are still good enough to be used over Ukraine as air defence, to shoot down Russian drones and missiles. “Because that is cheaper than using expensive and scarce Patriot missiles.”

articles.title: No ‘real proof’ Russia is preparing attack on NATO – Lithuanian PM (VIDEO)
articles.body:
No ‘real proof’ Russia is preparing attack on NATO – Lithuanian PM (VIDEO)
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius has said there is no evidence that Russia is preparing an attack on NATO territory, following a meeting with the military bloc’s chief, Mark Rutte, in Brussels.
His remarks came amid heightened tensions between Russia and NATO, as some Western officials and intelligence agencies have warned that Moscow could be preparing operations against member states in Europe.
At a press conference on Tuesday, an AFP reporter asked Sinkevicius, whose Baltic country borders Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, whether the “increasing hysteria and fear of hybrid attacks” could undermine Europe’s confidence and play into Russia’s hands.
“We’re not shaking. We’re not shivering. We are investing hugely in our defense capabilities,” Sinkevicius replied.
“I think it’s a must to say if the threat is there for the society. But you can’t exaggerate and say, ‘Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks,’” he added.
“I was addressing the secretary general [Rutte asking], ‘Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something?’ And there is actually none,” Sinkevicius said.
“The risk remains but it is not fluctuating, increasing or decreasing. We have to calmly do our work, and we’re doing it,” he added. His comments were also reported contemporaneously by international media.
👀 Lithuanian PM: "I was addressing the secretary general [Mark Rutte asking,] 'Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something?' And there is actually none."
In other words, most of the “OMG!… pic.twitter.com/2UdYUWWKPR
Rutte said the bloc should respond to potential threats by strengthening its own defenses and doing “even more for Ukraine, and not less.”
Speaking at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels the following day, the NATO chief similarly sought to play down fears of an imminent Russian attack.
“There is no imminent threat to NATO territory. If there is a build-up, we will see it and we will deal with it,” Rutte said.
European officials have increasingly discussed the possibility of a military confrontation with Russia, particularly around Kaliningrad, which is sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys argued in May that NATO must demonstrate its ability to “break into” the Russian exclave and destroy its air-defense and missile systems if necessary. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said last month that NATO members should closely monitor Russian forces in Kaliningrad and conduct exercises “so aggressively” that Moscow would be forced to divert troops from Ukraine to defend the region.
The Kremlin has described remarks about Kaliningrad as “borderline crazy,” while the Russian Embassy in Belgium condemned what it called “an unprecedented surge” in NATO military activity along Russia’s western borders.
“The Alliance is conducting a large-scale information campaign to propagate the myth of the ‘Russian threat’ and spread false information about Moscow’s alleged ‘intentions’ to attack one of the Baltic states by 2029 at the latest, or even sooner,” the Russian Embassy said on X on Monday.
It warned NATO members that “reckless and irresponsible” actions risked triggering a direct armed conflict.

articles.title: Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
articles.body:
Russia has a new warhead for its drones, and it is built to cut down power lines. For the first time, a jet drone has carried a shaped "cumulative-cutting" charge designed to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges, Serhii Beskrestnov, presidential adviser, known as Flash, said, as Russia opened its heaviest assault on Ukraine's power grid since last winter.
On 30 September, Russia launched its massed fall-winter campaign on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the last heating season, hitting power sites across 11 regions overnight with missiles and drones, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
The new warhead fits the aim: Flash says it is meant to bring down the high-voltage lines that carry the country's electricity. And Ukraine enters the winter exposed, with its energy resilience plans less than half complete.
A new charge targets the pylons
The device, which Flash calls a cumulative-cutting special load, is designed specifically to bring down high-voltage pylons and iron bridge structures.
"It consists of a main charge weighing 40 kilograms and four strike modules," he says.
In his reading, Russia intends to go after the major transmission lines that move power across the country, the backbone of the grid, rather than the substations it has struck before.
The campaign builds toward November
On 29 September, two senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Russia launched a three-part campaign of attacks on Kyiv, combining massive bombardments, sabotage, and the creation of political chaos. These efforts aimed at destabilizing the Ukrainian capital would peak by November, they said.
According to a representative of the Security Service of Ukraine, Russia has "thousands" of drones in its arsenal and is simultaneously expanding its stockpile of ballistic missiles. The plan is to "deploy the entire arsenal over the next two months," given that Ukraine lacks an effective weapon against jet-powered drones.

articles.title: Russia officially threatens NATO with nuclear weapons over Kaliningrad Oblast – Reuters
articles.body:
Russia officially threatens NATO with nuclear weapons over Kaliningrad Oblast – Reuters
Reuters, citing a document sent by Russia to NATO, has reported that Russia warned it is prepared to use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempts to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast.
Source: Reuters, as reported by European Pravda
Details: In the document, Moscow accused the alliance of pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" that carries "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict".
The document also referred to the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset".
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note quoted by Reuters says.
Meanwhile, a written response from NATO seen by Reuters said that NATO is a defensive alliance obliged to counter threats to its members from all directions.
Quote from NATO: "None of NATO's exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation. We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Background:
- Lithuania previously described Russia's new threats concerning Kaliningrad as psychological pressure.
- Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski believes NATO should step up military exercises near Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast.

articles.title: White House Taps Miller to Lead US Space Command
articles.body:
The White House has nominated Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. to lead U.S. Space Command, succeeding Gen. Stephen Whiting, who is expected to retire by January 2027.
A notice of Miller’s nomination for promotion to general appeared in the Congressional Record on Sept. 29, but the notice did not include an assignment. U.S. Space Command and the Space Force both confirmed Sept. 30 that Miller has been tapped for the SPACECOM commander job.
“Congratulations to Lt. Gen. Miller on his nomination to serve as Commander, U.S. Space Command,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said in a statement. “He is an exceptional Guardian who has represented our service with distinction, and we believe he is a strong candidate for this critical joint leadership role.”
Miller, currently the Space Force’s deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements, is a career space operator. He served as commander of Combat Forces Command—then Space Operations Command—from 2024 to 2025, and was director of operations, training, and force development at U.S. Space Command before that. Earlier in his career, he was chief of the Space Control Division within Air Force headquarters, led weapons and tactics development for the 21st Operations Group, and was an intercontinental ballistic missile operator and instructor.
His nomination would make him SPACEOM’s fourth leader since the command was reestablished in 2019, and its third to hail from the Space Force. Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence praised Miller as a “straightforward leader” and said he’s glad to see another Guardian in the top SPACECOM job.
“The unique relationship between the space-focused service and combatant command is undeniable,” Galbreath said. “I look forward to seeing that partnership continue to mature under the leadership of Gens. Schiess and Miller.”
If confirmed, Miller would take the reins of the command as the U.S. military’s reliance on space capabilities both in peacetime and in combat takes center stage—and as leaders increasingly emphasize the role of offensive operations in the domain.
Top Pentagon officials have said military space assets and SPACECOM forces played a key role in operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare, navigation, missile warning, and communications capabilities. Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed that the Space Force has “space control weapons”—the Defense Department’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. operates offensive systems in orbit.
Miller will also oversee construction of SPACECOM’s first purpose-built headquarters at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Ala., and the accompanying relocation of personnel and operations from Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The new facility is in the midst of a phased transition slated to conclude in 2031.
Whiting, the current SPACECOM commander, has been at the helm since January 2024. During his tenure, he has been a vocal proponent of better space domain awareness capabilities, a stronger space “kill chain,” and more dynamic, maneuverable satellites. In a recent speech at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii, he advocated for improved space-based target tracking and detection capabilities, which he said are foundational to the military’s ability to effectively perform space control operations.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said Sept. 16. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

articles.title: Russia sends NATO new nuclear threat over Kaliningrad as tensions rise
articles.body:
Russia told NATO it would be ready to use nuclear weapons if alliance members attempt to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart told the Kyiv Independent Sept. 30.
The warning came in a Russian non-paper delivered to NATO, which also threatened possible strikes against decision-making centers in NATO member states at the outset of such a conflict. The message adds to renewed Russian nuclear rhetoric toward Europe and warnings over hypothetical military action against the Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea.
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the note said.
It also raised the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
Hart rejected the threats, saying that NATO considers itself a defensive alliance and does not view its military activities as a threat to Russia.
"We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine," she said. "Russia's use of hybrid tactics is a sign of desperation. But we will not be dissuaded from our support to Ukraine."
The Russian Embassy in Ireland issued a similar warning on Sept. 30.
The embassy claimed that the European Union and NATO are increasing military activity along Russia's western border, including through military exercises. It also cited what it called "information" that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad Oblast, without providing evidence or identifying the source of the claim.
Kaliningrad Oblast is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, located between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
The embassy also pushed back against warnings from European officials that Moscow could be preparing for a military confrontation with Europe, saying there was no basis for such claims.
It cited Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov as saying that if the West attacks Russia, Moscow would respond with "a completely different war and a very brief one."
Russia has repeatedly used nuclear rhetoric in its confrontation with Western countries over its full-scale war against Ukraine. The U.K. has previously condemned Moscow's nuclear signaling as destabilizing and warned that such rhetoric increases the risk of miscalculation.
Western officials have also raised concerns over what they describe as growing Russian hybrid operations against NATO members, particularly countries on the alliance's eastern flank and those supporting Ukraine.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1680: Ukraine brings 14 more children home from occupied Kherson
articles.body:
Exclusives
Intelligence and technology
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest. Chains of Russian drones keep crossing near the Belarus border, Ukraine's Air Force says.
Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code. Each trainer assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges. Russia opens a massed assault on the grid.
Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach. A Ukrainian robot drives to the front, then swims.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module. The Mangal launcher carries two cameras, picks out drones on its own, and mounts on a vehicle or a fixed post.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters. Ukraine can jam Russian drones into drifting off course—a satellite relay overhead would let them fly straight through the jamming and strike.
International
EU wants reforms before more money. Kyiv wants Europe to touch Russia’s frozen billions. The push comes as Ukraine seeks access to €210 billion in immobilized Russian central-bank assets to help cover its needs.
Humanitarian and social impact
Ukraine brings 14 more children home from Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast. One of them was being forced onto Russia’s military rolls. This year's returns from the occupied south now reach 204.
Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram bomb while children in grades 1–4 were studying there. The bomb hit as about 40 children sheltered inside, one of many Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and villages over the past 24 hours.
Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter. Officials say the Kremlin is blending drone strikes, sabotage, and bot-farm propaganda to break the capital before the cold arrives.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says. One family in Oleshky was taken "to the basement" and has since disappeared without a trace, an Oleshky official says.

articles.title: Swedish Gripens to protect Ukraine aid hub in Poland
articles.body:
- Sweden will contribute Gripen fighters to NATO's integrated air and missile defense over Poland from October, Defense Minister Pål Jonson said.
- The jets will mainly operate from Sweden, with a smaller forward presence in Poland, to protect a logistics hub supporting Ukraine.
Sweden will send JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets back into NATO’s air defense mission over Poland from October, where they will help protect the hub in the country’s southeast that funnels military and civilian aid into Ukraine, Defense Minister Pål Jonson said on Sept. 30.
Most of the aircraft will fly from bases in Sweden, with only a smaller forward presence in Poland to support operations, Jonson wrote on X. Neither he nor the Swedish government said how many Gripens will take part or how long the deployment will last.
“Poland is a close ally and a vital hub for support to Ukraine. Swedish security is built together with our allies in NATO, and by taking responsibility together,” Jonson wrote.
The jets will join NATO’s integrated air and missile defense, the alliance’s network of fighters, radars and ground-based systems that watches for and intercepts aircraft, missiles and drones. Their main task is guarding the logistics hub in southeastern Poland, centered on the Rzeszów-Jasionka area near the Ukrainian border, through which much of the Western equipment bound for Ukraine passes.
“Repeated violations of NATO airspace underline the need for high readiness on the eastern flank,” Jonson wrote.
The most serious of those violations came in September 2025, when Polish and allied aircraft shot down Russian drones that crossed into Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine, the first time NATO jets had engaged Russian aircraft over alliance territory since the full-scale invasion began.
Swedish fighters have already guarded the same hub once before. After joining NATO in March 2024, Sweden sent six Gripens from its Norrbotten Wing to Malbork Air Base in northern Poland in March 2025 for NATO’s enhanced air policing mission, the first time Swedish combat aircraft operated from an ally’s territory. In May 2025, six more Gripen C fighters and about 120 personnel from the Blekinge Wing followed to protect the logistics hub that the new mission will cover.
The Gripen is a single-engine multirole fighter built by Saab, and its design emphasizes operating from dispersed bases and short runways with small ground crews, a feature suited to flying missions over Poland from home airfields in southern Sweden.
Swedish Gripens also flew NATO missions from Keflavik in Iceland in February and March 2026, and in August the Swedish broadcaster SVT reported that Stockholm planned to send Gripens and warships to help patrol Finland’s border with Russia, AeroTime reported.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 6, injure 34 across Ukraine as Kyiv faces another overnight missile, drone attack
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 6, injure 34 across Ukraine as Kyiv faces another overnight missile, drone attack
At least four people were killed and 30 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia launched another large-scale missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, local authorities said on Sept. 30.
Russia once again targeted Kyiv overnight, killing at least three people and injuring five others as daily Russian attacks on the capital continued, officials reported.
Just outside the capital in the neighbouring Kyiv Oblast, at least one child was found killed under the rubble of a home in Vyshhorod, Kyiv Oblast Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko said. A man and a woman also suffered injuries amid the attack.
The Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with Zircon and Onyx anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles, and 188 attack drones of various types, including 86 jet-powered drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 160 aerial targets, including five missiles and 155 drones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 18 locations.
In northern Sumy Oblast, two people were killed and at least 15 others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local authorities said. A 74-year-old man and a 70-year-old woman were killed after guided aerial bombs struck the Sumy.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, five people were injured as Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure and residential areas, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Two houses were damaged.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured a 67-year-old man over the past day, regional authorities said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 20 times with aerial bombs, drones, and artillery, also causing a fire.

articles.title: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
articles.body:
On the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop. The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.
Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”
Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China.
Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of the Chinese volunteers project.
“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”
Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.
Ukraine’s military is facing an acute manpower shortage. Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits: foreigners.
There are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July, Mykhailo Fedorov passed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.
But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.
On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.
On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing has increased trade links with Moscow to record levels since 2022 and provided diplomatic support on numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.
Some people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.
Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.
Plus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.
Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.
Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.
But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.
Vanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.
Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.
Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s own economic downturn. His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.
He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”
Other members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.
He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.
“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”
His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.
Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.
All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.
Whatever contribution they may ultimately make towards peace, or to war, as Chinese nationals their decision is likely to have consequences that last beyond the conflict that they are now a part of. On 23 September, one of their Chinese comrades in the unit was killed in a Russian attack. Upon hearing the news, one volunteer, a doctor, decided to leave. The rest, said Nero, insisted on staying.
Additional research by Illia Dyadik, Yu-chen Li and Artem Mazhulin

articles.title: Russia Launches New Wave of Massive Strikes on Ukraine’s Energy Infrastructure
articles.body:
During the night of September 30, Russia launched a massive missile-and-drone attack on energy infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Monitoring resources eRadar and War Monitor reported strikes on energy facilities.
During the attack, they tracked ballistic and high-speed missiles heading toward the capital and energy infrastructure.
There were also reports of Russian drones flying toward and descending near energy facilities, including the area around Kyiv’s CHPP-5.
As of 9:30 a.m., the attack was still ongoing, and the air raid alert in Kyiv had not yet been lifted.
Ukrenergo also confirmed the attack’s impact on energy infrastructure, saying some consumers were without power in the morning and that crews had already begun emergency restoration work.
Later, the Ukrainian Air Force reported that during the night of September 30, Russia used Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles, as well as 188 Shahed, Gerbera, Parodiya, and other types of attack drones against Ukraine. Of the drones used in the attack, 86 were jet-powered.
As of 8:00 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 160 targets, including five ballistic/high-speed missiles and 155 drones.
According to War Monitor’s estimates, Russia used 10 3M22 Zircon/3M55 Oniks-M missiles and another six 9M723 Iskander-M/RM-48U ballistic missiles launched from S-400 systems against Kyiv and its suburbs.
The attack came less than a week after Russia’s previous large-scale use of ballistic missiles against Kyiv.
Militarnyi previously reported that on the night of September 24, Russia launched three waves of attacks on the capital using Zircon and Iskander missiles, as well as attack drones.
According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian air defenses intercepted around 60% of the ballistic missiles used in that attack.
