articles.title: Trump expected to resume major Iran war after midterms – Axios
articles.body:
Trump expected to resume major Iran war after midterms – Axios
American officials believe US President Donald Trump could order a resumption of major combat operations against Iran after the midterm elections in November, as renewed indirect negotiations produced no results, Axios reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Qatari mediators, who met separately with US and Iranian negotiators in New York on Monday, are reportedly growing increasingly frustrated that neither side is willing to make concessions.
“It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the US can’t accept and the US thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise,” Axios cited a source as saying.
Trump rejected Iran’s latest proposal last week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG deliveries. He has since denied reports that he was ready to provide sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian assets in exchange for concessions on Iran’s nuclear program. “I offered them NOTHING,” he wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
Democrats are ahead of Republicans by more than ten points nationally in the race for control of the US House of Representatives, according to recent polls by Quinnipiac University and NPR/PBS/Marist.
The war launched by the US and Israel against Iran on February 28 has been unpopular among American voters overall. It sharply divided Trump’s base, with some critics arguing that the president violated his promise of “no new wars” and his stated opposition to “forever wars.”
The relentless bombing campaign failed to subdue Iran and, according to the Pentagon’s inspector general, significantly depleted US ammunition stockpiles. Disruptions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continue to drive energy prices, which Trump recently attempted to blame on the Ukraine conflict.
“Donald Trump cannot calm energy markets or conceal the costs of his blockade and hostile policies through show-off and social media posts,” an Iranian security official told RT last week.
According to a recent Fox News poll, 71% of registered voters in the US believed that the Trump administration lacked “a clear strategy for ending the war with Iran,” while 60% said the US had made the wrong decision to launch military action.
The poll also found that 47% of respondents believed military action against Iran would make the US less safe, while 32% said it would make the country safer.

articles.title: Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
articles.body:
Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
TEHRAN — Iran has received Washington’s response to its latest initiative aimed at ending the seven-month-long conflict that began with unprovoked, joint US-Israeli strikes on February 28, as President Donald Trump remains stubbornly wedded to the delusion that military pressure and economic warfare can force the Islamic Republic into submission.
The US response was submitted to President Masoud Pezeshkian during a Cabinet session on Wednesday by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani confirmed.
Addressing the Cabinet, President Pezeshkian reaffirmed Tehran’s principled position on resolving the crisis through diplomacy without compromising fundamental rights.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said, emphasizing: “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The development follows Araghchi’s return from the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where Iranian diplomats engaged in indirect exchanges with American representatives while holding intensive consultations on the sidelines with Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Mohajerani noted that Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on these diplomatic engagements, which detailed Iran’s framework for reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Last week, Araghchi presented a comprehensive seven-point proposal to reopen the waterway within seven days, contingent upon Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, unfreezing national assets, and removing illegal sanctions on Iranian oil exports. While Trump hastily dismissed the initiative—claiming Iran was “losing so badly” and that Tehran’s terms “would not be acceptable”—regional mediators have persisted in their efforts to forge a diplomatic resolution based on the reality on the ground.
Paralyzed by strategic deadlock
Tehran views Washington’s mixed signals not as strength, but as profound strategic disorientation. Speaking on Tuesday during a meeting in Tehran with Shahin Mustafayev, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), characterized the US president as trapped in a state of absolute paralysis.
“Trump is caught in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight,” Rezaei stated. “Iran’s conditions have been conveyed to the United States, but Trump is unable to make a decision, and the United States, out of desperation, has resorted to an air siege in the military war.”
Denouncing the initial February 28 aggression as a blatant violation of international law, Rezaei noted that Iran “powerfully defended itself,” citing the hundreds of precise drone and missile retaliatory strikes conducted by the Iranian Armed Forces against US and Israeli military installations across the region. Tehran has repeatedly cautioned Washington that it will never leave any act of aggression unanswered, demonstrating through seven months of sustained resistance that its deterrence remains fully intact.
This is not the first time Washington has squandered diplomatic off-ramps. Following the collapse of the fragile April 8 ceasefire and the subsequent Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) brokered on June 17, Tehran has demonstrated a readiness to engage in serious diplomacy if national sovereignty is respected. President Pezeshkian reiterated his commitment to seeing the Islamabad MoU come to fruition while safeguarding vital national interests, rejecting US bullying: “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”
From military failure to psychological warfare
Having failed to break Iran’s defensive capabilities, the US and Israel have shifted their tactics toward internal disruption. Addressing mayors of major metropolitan centers and provincial capitals on Tuesday, President Pezeshkian pointed out that Washington and Tel Aviv have pivoted toward hybrid subversion after suffering strategic setbacks on the battlefield.
“After failing to force the Iranian people to surrender through military war, enemies have focused their entire plan on creating and intensifying internal divisions,” Pezeshkian cautioned.
Despite this dual track of subversion and rhetoric, the White House continues to escalate coercive measures. On Tuesday, the US Treasury Department unveiled fresh sanctions under its so-called “Operation Economic Outcast,” blacklisting ten individuals and entities across Iran, Hong Kong, and Pakistan over alleged roles in Iran’s defense procurement.
Trump’s search for an off-ramp
However, the coercive campaign has boomeranged disastrously onto the US domestic arena. With US legislative elections just five weeks away, polls indicate that Trump’s war against Iran has been overwhelmingly unpopular from its inception. The disruption of Persian Gulf transit corridors and the subsequent spike in global crude prices have placed immense strain on American households, threatening Republican control of both chambers of Congress.
In a stark illustration of the domestic fallout, California Governor Gavin Newsom suspended the state’s seasonal summer-blend gasoline requirement, directing regulatory bodies to immediately permit the distribution of cheaper winter-blend fuel. In just seven months, Trump’s war has drained over $120 billion in extra fuel expenses from American consumers—imposing an estimated $428 burden on every California household and eroding US economic stability.
With domestic outrage mounting, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) directly addressed the American public on Tuesday in an unprecedented 26-page open letter, calling on voters to reject the architects of the conflict.
“Remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians who are responsible for America’s current state,” the IRGC stated, adding: “Make sure your politicians understand that the world has changed.”
While Donald Trump is desperately seeking an off-ramp before voters head to the polls, analysts emphasize that any genuine breakthrough will remain elusive until Washington completely discards the Israeli-instigated illusion that Iran can be coerced into capitulation. Until the White House frees itself from Tel Aviv’s maximalist adventurism and faces strategic realities, its policies will remain locked in the very quagmire of its own making.

articles.title: Iran warns regional states against hosting Israeli officials after Netanyahu’s UAE visit
articles.body:
Iran warns regional states against hosting Israeli officials after Netanyahu’s UAE visit
TEHRAN – Iran has warned regional countries about the consequences of the presence of destabilizing actors such as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on their soils, warning about Tel Aviv’s efforts to sow regional tensions.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry issued the remarks in a statement on Tuesday, reacting to reports of Netanyahu’s presence in the UAE at the official invitation of Emirati ruler Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
It strongly condemned the “child-killing and war-mongering prime minister of the Israeli regime’s provocative presence” in the region and warned of the “extremely dangerous consequences.”
The ministry noted that “regional security is a collective and indivisible matter,” warning that facilitating the entry of destabilizing actors could lead to “greater division, insecurity, and instability in West Asia.”
It called on regional governments to “refrain from facilitating the Israeli regime’s destabilizing presence” and to prevent their territories from becoming “a platform for destabilizing actions against other countries in the region.”
The statement reminded that the region was experiencing “one of the most fragile and sensitive periods in its history,” citing the regime’s “proven hostility and animosity towards Iran and other countries in the region” and its “repeated threats” against the Islamic Republic.
“All countries in the region must be vigilant about the consequences and repercussions of such a presence, which threatens regional peace and collective security,” the ministry said.
The strong rebuke followed reports by Israeli media and statements from senior Israeli officials to Reuters confirming that Netanyahu paid a visit to Abu Dhabi on Sunday, holding closed-door consultations with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan for most of the day before returning to Tel Aviv.
The trip was initially kept under wraps. Late on Monday, the United Arab Emirates officially confirmed that Netanyahu had met with Sheikh Mohamed over the weekend. Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 was the first to break news of the visit, prompting Israel’s internal security agency, Shin Bet, to file an immediate complaint with the military censor over alleged breaches of operational secrecy.
According to Reuters, the weekend trip was not Netanyahu’s first covert foray into Abu Dhabi; the Israeli premier had also traveled secretly to the Persian Gulf state on March 26 for closed-door discussions with the Emirati leadership.
Normalization as an instrument of destabilization
Ties between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv were formalized in 2020 through the controversial, US-brokered Abraham Accords. While marketed by Washington and Abu Dhabi as an engine for regional “peace and prosperity,” the normalization drive has systematically functioned as a mechanism to fracture Islamic and regional unity, undermine the Palestinian liberation struggle, and embed the Zionist regime directly along the strategic waterways of the Persian Gulf.
Over the past four years, the UAE has evolved into Israel’s primary operational, logistical, and commercial bridgehead in the immediate neighborhood. Rather than fostering regional coexistence, Abu Dhabi’s entente with Tel Aviv has exacerbated regional fault lines.
Strategic and military integration between the two sides has deepened rapidly. In May, United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee stated that Israel had deployed Iron Dome air defense batteries and operational personnel directly to the UAE. The presence of Israeli military hardware and intelligence operatives on Emirati soil represents a direct violation of regional security arrangements and a blatant concession of Persian Gulf sovereign territory to an expansionist entity actively carrying out genocidal aggression against the Palestinian people in Gaza and escalating confrontations across the regional front.
Political observers have repeatedly warned that the UAE’s willingness to outsource its defense architecture to Tel Aviv compromises the collective security of all littoral states. By permitting Israeli intelligence agencies and military hardware to establish footprints just kilometers away from Iranian shores, Abu Dhabi is transforming the Persian Gulf from a zone of peaceful commerce and sovereign cooperation into a theater of Zionist espionage and provocation.
A pattern of malign regional intervention
The welcoming of Netanyahu into the Emirati capital is seen by analysts as part of a wider, destructive pattern defining Abu Dhabi’s regional foreign policy over the past decade.
Across West Asia and North Africa, the UAE has repeatedly operated as a destabilizing force, pursuing interventionist agendas that have fueled sectarian friction, funded mercenary proxy networks, and undermined sovereign central governments.
From its active participation in the devastating, years-long war of aggression against Yemen—which created one of the worst humanitarian catastrophes of the modern era—to its illegal occupation of strategic Yemeni islands such as Socotra and Mayyun, Abu Dhabi has sought to unilaterally dominate maritime chokepoints along the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Extensive reports have revealed that the UAE has facilitated Israeli intelligence installations on Socotra, leveraging occupied Yemeni territories to project joint Israeli-Emirati influence over vital international shipping corridors.
Beyond the Arabian Peninsula, Abu Dhabi’s footprint has proven equally destructive in the Horn of Africa and North Africa. In Sudan, the UAE has drawn fierce international condemnation for arming and financing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), whose campaign has pushed the country into devastating civil war and famine. In Libya, Emirati financial and military backing for renegade military factions severely derailed United Nations peace efforts for years.
By tying its regional ambitions to Tel Aviv’s geopolitical objectives, the UAE is effectively functioning as a sub-imperial vector for Western and Zionist interests, attempting to displace the organic, sovereign mechanisms of indigenous regional diplomacy in favor of imported, militarized alliances.
The secretive summit in Abu Dhabi also underscores Netanyahu’s desperate drive to manufacture diplomatic breakthroughs abroad to stave off mounting domestic collapse at home.
Facing intense internal turmoil and trailing sharply in domestic polls ahead of Knesset elections, the beleaguered Israeli prime minister is confronting fierce political challenges.
Facing persistent corruption trials and widespread public outrage over his regime’s strategic failures in Gaza and the North, Netanyahu is exploiting ties with Abu Dhabi as a political lifeline. By rolling out the red carpet for a war criminal wanted for crimes against humanity, Abu Dhabi is not only shielding Netanyahu from international isolation but actively facilitating his political survival.

articles.title: ‘If people are in a bunker, business stops’: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses
articles.body:
Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.
Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.
“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.
Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.
To ease the economic costs, the government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts.
A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.
More than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts, Kravchenko said.
But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.
It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.
Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.
The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.
To protect against future strikes, the government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.
The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.
Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.
Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year, Kravchenko said.
“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.
Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.
Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.
“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.
But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50% of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40%. The same survey found that 72% believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.
Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but admitted that Ukraine faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.
“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.
Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, according to the minister, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.
Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”
“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.

articles.title: Pentagon buys Israeli smart rifle sights to shoot down drones
articles.body:
- JIATF-401 awarded Smart Shooter a three-year, sole-supplier contract worth up to $150 million for SMASH counter-drone rifle sights.
- The contract supports the task force's Domestic Shield Program to protect U.S. forces and bases at home and abroad.
The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force has awarded Israeli company Smart Shooter a contract worth up to $150 million for its SMASH rifle sights, which help soldiers shoot down small drones with their regular service weapons.
The U.S. Department of War’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, known as JIATF-401, announced the three-year award on Sept. 29, and Smart Shooter said the next day that it is the only supplier under the deal. The contract is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity agreement, which sets a ceiling and lets the government place individual orders over time. The quantity, pricing and timing of deliveries will be decided in those orders, and neither the company nor the task force said how many systems the first order will cover.
The contract covers SMASH hardware, software and updates, training and support. It supports JIATF-401’s Domestic Shield Program and related missions overseas, focused on protecting troops, bases and other key sites in the United States and abroad from drones.
SMASH is a fire control system that mounts on a rifle like a scope. It uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to lock onto a target, calculate where to aim and release the shot only when the weapon is lined up to hit. That lets an ordinary soldier hit a small, fast-moving drone that would be very hard to shoot down with iron sights or a standard optic. The rifle can still be used normally against ground targets, and the soldier decides whether to fire. The system can also link to outside sensors and battle management networks.
“Domestic Shield is about giving defenders the tools to stop small, fast-moving drones before they can harm forces, bases, and critical assets,” said Michal Mor, CEO and co-founder of Smart Shooter.
JIATF-401 coordinates counter-drone work across the U.S. military and federal agencies. The task force is led by U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross.
“Our approach allows us to identify the right capabilities for specific operational requirements and rapidly deliver those capabilities to the warfighter,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401.
The award is Smart Shooter’s second with the task force, following a contract announced in March 2026. The company says thousands of SMASH systems are already in use across the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Marine Corps, and that it has won a series of new and follow-on orders from those services over the past year. SMASH is also used by forces in Israel, the United Kingdom, Germany and other NATO and allied countries.
JIATF-401 has been signing larger counter-drone deals this year. In May, it gave Perennial Autonomy a three-year contract worth up to $500 million for interceptor drones, including the Merops system that U.S. forces have used against Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones, DroneXL reported.
Smart Shooter, founded in Israel, has offices in the United States, Europe and Australia.

articles.title: Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest
articles.body:
Russia is wiring its long-range attack drones together by a mesh network in flight and buying pricier, higher-resolution cameras for them, Ukraine's Air Force reported on 29 September. Its spokesperson said one drone could serve as a scout, strike drone, and relay for the rest, which is why they often fly one behind another over long distances. Chains of them keep crossing near the Belarus border, UkrInform reports.
For Ukraine, the danger in each such upgrade is arithmetic: the more Russia networks cheap, once-disposable drones and pushes its control links away from the front, the harder they become to jam or shoot down, and the more of them reach the cities they are aimed at.
Sharper, pricier eyes
Ihnat said on a national broadcast that Russia is sourcing higher-quality materials and raising the resolution of its drone cameras. The cameras it buys are increasingly expensive and higher-quality, he said, which lets its operators study the ground in fine detail and use each drone for a specific purpose.
On a mesh network, he said, the drones talk to each other and hand the control signal back toward the operator, so no single link has to carry it alone.
Russia is mapping everyday targets across Kyiv, from trolleybus depots to Zhuliany airport, top monitoring channel says, ahead of next ballistic strike
Chains along the Belarus border
Asked about relays operating out of Belarus and about Russia's guidance of jet-powered Shaheds, the exploding drones it fires in swarms, Ihnat said Moscow had already claimed its satellite network was ready. He confirmed mesh networks are in use and said their use was quite dangerous. Ukraine has no information yet on whether Russia is using towers, he said.
It often sees drones crossing long distances in chains along the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, so nothing can be ruled out, but intelligence would have to confirm whether such relays exist. Asked whether Russia is preparing a fresh ballistic strike, he said intelligence would warn when extra vigilance is needed.
Ukraine's countermeasures
Ihnat has also said Russia launched more attack drones in September than in August, counting 3,177 jet-powered drones so far this month against 2,850 in August. To knock them down, Ukraine leans mainly on tactical aviation, including F-16 fighters, and on ground-based air defense when missiles are available, he said, with shoulder-fired man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) working well against jet drones inside their range. He said Ukraine needs more missiles for both Patriot systems and ground-based launchers, plus faster domestic solutions it can scale up.

articles.body:
The EU is putting money into the places inside Ukraine where the army trains its soldiers. The bloc will fund the modernization of several military training centers in Ukraine, upgrading facilities, housing, and equipment, with Denmark administering the funds and the Come Back Alive charity carrying out the work, the Defense Ministry said.

The money goes into the centers

Halan calls training a foundation
The aim is a modern environment for preparing soldiers.
"Modernized centers let us train the military on real combat experience," Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan says, thanking the EU and every partner country.
Training inside Ukraine, she says, is as fundamental to defense as ammunition and equipment, because weapons do not work without people trained to use them. The modernized sites, the ministry says, are meant to let Ukraine prepare its own forces to a higher standard, faster, and closer to the front.
Denmark administers the funds
The project is an EU initiative, open to any partner willing to contribute, with Denmark as the fund administrator. The ministry thanked the EU, Denmark, and Come Back Alive for support it says raises the quality of Ukraine's training.

articles.title: STARK Unveils Vanta 12 USV With 1,200-Nautical-Mile Range and 10 Kamikaze Drones
articles.body:
German company STARK has presented its new unmanned surface vessel (USV), the Vanta 12.
STARK told Militarnyi about the new USV.
The Vanta 12 is designed to conduct reconnaissance and surveillance, electronic warfare (EW), maritime area patrols, and strike missions.
The unmanned surface vessel is 12 meters long, can reach speeds over 40 knots, and has a range of up to 1,200 nautical miles (approximately 2,222 km). Its stated payload capacity is up to two tonnes.
According to the developer, the vessel is designed to remain at sea for several weeks without returning to base.
“Hybrid threats are challenging because they often lack a clear point of onset. Suspicious activity near a cable or energy facility does not necessarily indicate an attack, but it is important to detect such activity in a timely manner, monitor how the situation develops, and respond rapidly. Therefore, persistent maritime presence and surveillance are becoming increasingly important to protect critical infrastructure. Given the growing use of unmanned aerial systems, the ability to conduct electronic warfare at sea is becoming equally important,” Maksym Cherkis, Chief Operating Officer of STARK Ukraine, shared.
The platform uses autonomous navigation and software incorporating AI capabilities. Its modular architecture allows for the integration of various sensor suites, electronic warfare systems, and weapons.
The unmanned platform is controlled using Minerva, a system the company developed to integrate remotely operated systems of different types into a unified command-and-control architecture.
The Vanta 12 is equipped with ten Cascade loitering munitions developed by STARK, which were publicly unveiled at the Eurosatory international defense exhibition in June. The company has also launched the munitions from a maritime platform.
The loitering munition is launched from a dedicated tubular container. The Cascade has a maximum flight range of up to 100 km, a cruising speed of approximately 100 km/h, and a terminal dive speed of up to 220 km/h. Its payload capacity can reach 4.5 kg.
In addition, the Vanta 12 has been integrated with four Sea Venom anti-ship missiles manufactured by MBDA. These lightweight anti-ship missiles were jointly developed by the United Kingdom and France and are designed to engage surface targets, including corvette-class warships.
The Vanta 12’s capabilities were tested in September during the REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal. REPMUS is an annual large-scale exercise and experimentation program focused on robotic and unmanned maritime systems, organized by the Portuguese Navy with the participation of NATO structures and the European Defence Agency.
During REPMUS, the Vanta 12 operated alongside crewed and other unmanned platforms. According to STARK, the vessel conducted simulated combat scenarios, while the Minerva system controlled the platform and launched the Cascade loitering munitions.
STARK is a European defense technology company that develops and manufactures unmanned systems for air and maritime operations, as well as software for their control and management. The company operates in Germany, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Greece, and Sweden.
The Vanta 12 is a further development of STARK’s family of unmanned surface vessels, which also includes smaller platforms. In August, the company delivered the first Seetaube unmanned surface vessel to the German Armed Forces. The vessel was developed on the Vanta platform.
To scale up production of the Vanta family, STARK is partnering with German shipbuilder Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft (FSG). The companies plan to expand the industrial base for manufacturing these platforms in Germany and other European countries.
Militarnyi previously reported on the opening of STARK’s Ukrainian R&D center and the delivery of Virtus strike drones to Ukraine, which had previously undergone testing in combat conditions.

articles.title: ‘Trump is trapped’: Qatar pushes Iran compromise as US warns fighting could resume after midterms
articles.body:
Qatar is intensifying efforts to broker a breakthrough between the United States and Iran and bring an end to their seven-month war, but the latest round of indirect talks has produced little progress. U.S. officials believe the deepening stalemate is increasing the likelihood of renewed military confrontation, with some assessing that President Donald Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterm elections, Axios reported. 
Trump again insisted Tuesday that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and suggested the conflict would ultimately end on Washington’s terms. “They are doing very poorly. I don’t know if they are ready to give up yet. They will give up. This is to stop a nuclear weapon. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon,” he told reporters. 
Iran, meanwhile, accused Washington of being unable to choose between diplomacy and war. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Trump was “trapped in a quagmire in which he can neither negotiate nor fight,” according to Iranian media cited by Axios. 
Despite the increasingly sharp rhetoric, Qatar has not abandoned the diplomatic track. Qatari officials are expected to continue shuttling messages between the sides even as frustration grows in Doha over their refusal to compromise. Qatar previously played a central role in securing the June memorandum of understanding that briefly halted the fighting before the arrangement later unraveled. 
On Monday, Qatari mediators held separate talks with Iranian and U.S. officials. According to Axios, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his team spent several hours discussing a two-page Qatari compromise proposal before Qatari representatives traveled to Washington for talks with Trump administration officials. 
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said Doha was continuing to pass messages between the parties and search for common ground. “We are conveying messages between the sides and working to find common ground in order to reach an agreement,” he said. “Only that will save us all from the consequences of the conflict.”
The Qatari proposal is aimed at bridging the two central disputes separating Washington and Tehran. Iran wants the United States to lift its naval blockade, while the Trump administration is demanding concrete Iranian concessions on the nuclear program. U.S. officials had initially described Monday’s contacts as “positive and constructive” and said Tehran appeared willing to show flexibility on nuclear issues, but by the end of the day there had been no significant movement. 
Talks remain ‘stuck’
“It is stuck,” one source familiar with the talks told Axios. “The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can’t accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise.” Pakistan and Egypt have also urged Tehran to make concessions on its nuclear program, while Iran has insisted it will consider such steps only after Washington returns to the terms of the June memorandum. 
The dispute has also exposed conflicting messages from Washington. U.S. officials told Axios earlier this week that Trump was prepared to offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange for concrete measures to curb Tehran’s nuclear program. Trump later rejected that account on Truth Social, writing that he had offered Iran nothing. 
Preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remains one of Trump’s stated objectives in the war. He has also described weakening Tehran’s ability to threaten neighboring countries as a U.S. goal.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly presented UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan with what an Israeli source described to CNN as new intelligence indicating that Iran has resumed progress on its nuclear program. According to the report, the material included information about new construction at the so-called Pickaxe Mountain site, about 140 miles south of Tehran, which Israel views as a potentially important location in any effort to rebuild Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. The UAE publicly confirmed Netanyahu’s visit, though its official account said the meeting focused on bilateral ties and regional developments. 
Separately, Iranian authorities reported Wednesday that Ali Hemmati and Majid Nikandish, two people detained over anti-government protests earlier this year, had been executed after being convicted in connection with the deaths of four security personnel in Mashhad. Human rights groups had previously listed Nikandish among protesters facing execution, though independent verification of the circumstances surrounding the case remains limited.

The emergency services said a child was found dead under the rubble of a residential building that was destroyed in the wider Kiev region.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.

“After failing to force the Iranian people to surrender through military war, enemies have focused their entire plan on creating and intensifying internal divisions,” Pezeshkian stated.
Underscoring the critical necessity of national unity, the president warned against political monopolism, noting: “A group must not weaken the country under the illusion that they are ‘all-knowing’; public participation by all citizens is the most important way to overcome conspiracies.”
Pezeshkian’s remarks come in the wake of the major military confrontation that erupted on February 28, during which joint US-Israeli strikes and regional escalations were met with comprehensive retaliatory missile and drone operations by Iranian armed forces. Iran has established operational deterrence and retained the upper hand during the conflict, demonstrating advanced air defense capabilities and the capacity to project precision firepower against critical adversary infrastructure across the region.
The military deadlock and subsequent failure to achieve operational objectives—such as neutralizing Iran’s strategic assets—have forced Washington and Tel Aviv to recalibrate their posture. Facing domestic political fallout and strategic exhaustion following the February clashes, the US-Israeli alliance has increasingly shifted focus toward hybrid warfare, economic pressure, and psychological operations aimed at fracturing domestic consensus in Iran.
Iranian leadership across both civilian and military branches has consistently maintained that internal cohesion remains the primary pillar underpinning the country’s defense doctrine. In his address, Pezeshkian called on local administrators and municipal leaders to actively engage local populations, address socioeconomic challenges transparently, and reinforce public trust to neutralize covert foreign destabilization efforts designed to compensate for adversary defeats on the conventional battlefield.

articles.title: Belgium Orders NASAMS to Protect Strategic Sites
articles.body:
Belgium has ordered medium-range NASAMS air defense systems from Norwegian company Kongsberg to strengthen the protection of its strategically important military and infrastructure sites.
The defense company’s press service reported this.
The contract, worth kr10 billion (approximately €918 million), was signed with the Netherlands Armed Forces’ procurement agency on behalf of Belgium.
“We are very pleased to welcome Belgium to the family of NASAMS nations,” Eirik Lie, President and CEO of KONGSBERG, said.
He noted that acquiring these SAM systems will provide Belgium with reliable nationwide air defense coverage and help strengthen overall European security.
In late February, Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Belgium would receive NASAMS air defense systems, which it plans to deploy to protect the Port of Antwerp, Europe’s second-busiest port.
The government moved to procure the new SAM systems after the country faced numerous incidents of unknown drones flying over strategic sites in 2025.
Drones were also spotted over the Port of Antwerp, nuclear power plants, BASF’s chemical plant, and the Europa container terminal. Following these incidents, in early November, Belgian armed forces personnel were ordered to shoot down any unidentified drones over military bases.
Belgium’s Ministry of Defense reported that the first part of the NASAMS will become operational in 2027. This will allow nearly two-thirds of the port area to be protected.
The NASAMS air defense system consists of a command post, an AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel radar for detection and guidance, launchers carrying six missiles each, and specialized vehicles for reloading and maintenance.
The system’s primary interceptors are AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles, which, depending on the variant, can engage targets at ranges of up to 40 km. The system can also use short-range AIM-9 Sidewinder guided missiles and specialized AMRAAM-ER missiles with an extended range.

articles.title: U.S. Army signs $4.15B in anti-drone deals with 10 firms
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army awarded 10 companies counter-drone contracts with a combined ceiling of $4.15 billion on Sept. 28, 2026.
- Seven firms received $500 million ceilings, two received $250 million and one $150 million, with funding set by individual orders through September 2029.
The U.S. Army has awarded 10 companies counter-drone contracts with a combined ceiling of $4.15 billion, lining up commercial radars, cameras, jammers and weapons to detect and defeat hostile drones, the U.S. Department of War announced.
Seven companies received ceilings of $500 million each: Allen Control Systems of Austin, Texas; Digital Force Technologies of San Diego; DroneShield’s U.S. arm in Warrenton, Virginia; Napatree Technology of McLean, Virginia; RADA Technologies of Germantown, Maryland; SRC of Syracuse, New York; and Wescam USA of Nashville, Tennessee. Echodyne of Kirkland, Washington, and PVP Advanced EO Systems of Lake Forest, California, received $250 million each, and Smart Shooter of Herndon, Virginia, received $150 million.
All 10 firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts were awarded on Sept. 28 by Army Contracting Command at Detroit Arsenal, Michigan, and run through late September 2029. The figures are ceilings on what the U.S. Army can order from each company over three years, and work locations and funding will be set order by order. The Pentagon’s notices describe the work only as commercial counter-unmanned aerial systems and counter small-unmanned aerial systems capabilities, without naming the products the service intends to buy. The solicitation, posted online, drew 50 bids.
The overall contract vehicle could eventually be worth as much as $7 billion, Breaking Defense reported. U.S. Army acquisition chief Brent Ingraham told reporters the awards span sensors, weapons to defeat drones, and command and control systems, and will also support counter-drone needs elsewhere in the federal government.
Only a small share of the money has been committed. Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Army-led office coordinating counter-drone work across the Pentagon, said $50 million had been obligated across the 10 contracts as of Sept. 29, DefenseScoop reported. The task force has now awarded more than $5 billion in counter-drone contracts overall, including earlier deals of roughly $500 million each with AeroVironment and CACI.
The contracts feed the Pentagon’s drone and counter-drone marketplaces, which officials describe as commercial-style hubs where local, state, federal and some allied customers can buy equipment. They also support Domestic Shield, the task force’s program to protect U.S. military bases and critical infrastructure from small drones. Matt Ross, who leads the task force, has said the U.S. Army wants layered defenses able to detect, track, identify and defeat hostile drones.
The winners cover different parts of that chain. On the detection side, RADA Technologies, a unit of Leonardo DRS, builds compact radars designed specifically to find small drones, and its sensors already equip the U.S. Army’s Mobile Short-Range Air Defense system on the Stryker and the U.S. Marine Corps’ Marine Air Defense Integrated System. Echodyne makes compact electronically scanned radars used for drone detection and perimeter security, while SRC works on radar and electronic warfare systems. Wescam USA belongs to L3Harris and makes the WESCAM MX family of stabilized electro-optical and infrared camera turrets used to spot and track targets.
On the defeat side, DroneShield, an Australian company, sells radio-frequency detection systems and jammers that break the link between a drone and its operator. Allen Control Systems builds Bullfrog, an autonomous gun turret that uses computer vision to aim a machine gun at drones. Smart Shooter, an Israeli company with a U.S. subsidiary, makes the SMASH fire-control sight, which helps soldiers hit small drones with ordinary rifles. Napatree Technology is listed in the Pentagon’s notice as a small business.

articles.title: ‘No way they can beat us’: Rutte rebuffs Russian nuclear threats to NATO
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday issued a strong rebuke to Russia after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.
"We had to reply and make clear to [Russia] that NATO is a defensive alliance ... and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it's not helpful," Rutte said at a security summit in Brussels. "NATO is so much stronger than Russia is, so there's no way they can ever beat us."
"The best way to deal with this is to have a little bit of calm," he added. "That's the message: calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going — that's how we deal with it."
Advertisement
Rutte's unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.
In recent days, Russia's embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying "reckless and irresponsible" behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.
"We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the embassy wrote on social media.
In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.
NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance's spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.
"We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," she said in a statement. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Advertisement
Inside NATO, some allies are dismissing the threat. "Our reading is that they want to intimidate allied public opinion so that allies stop supporting [Ukraine], while, at the same time, presenting NATO as the one that would be responsible for an eventual escalation," said the same NATO diplomat cited above. "Textbook Russian propaganda."
"Russia always accelerates when it's the most guilty or when [it] loses," said a second alliance diplomat. "So they are cornered now and they transfer the blame on NATO."
Russia's embassy to Belgium didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
articles.body:
Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN again, two years after severing diplomatic ties with Kiev over a rebel ambush that killed dozens of Malian soldiers and allied Russian forces.
Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop told the UN General Assembly on Monday that Ukraine was aiding armed groups in the Sahel and urged the international community to respond.
Why has Mali raised the accusation again?
Diop’s remarks follow a series of coordinated militant raids in Mali and new reports of Ukrainian assistance with drone operations. Pointing to attacks on April 25 and July 4, he said they exposed a “dangerous connection” between jihadists and separatist rebels, and accused Kiev of aiding forces that threaten his country’s territorial integrity.
“Ukraine is just the visible part of the iceberg,” he said, claiming the violence was part of a wider effort to destabilize the Sahel states and obstruct their break with former colonial influence.
The April offensive by the Al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) struck several cities and killed Malian Defense Minister Sadio Camara. Mali’s army said it repelled assaults on military sites and key infrastructure with support from Russia’s Africa Corps, killing more than 200 militants.
Malian Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maiga described the offensive as an attempt to seize power. The Russian Defense Ministry acknowledged the assault, saying it amounted to an attempted coup and claimed that the attackers had received training involving Ukrainian and European mercenary instructors.
How did the dispute with Ukraine begin?
In July 2024, Tuareg rebels ambushed Malian troops and Wagner Group contractors near Tinzaouaten, close to the Algerian border. Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov later said the rebels had received “necessary information” that enabled the operation, adding that “there will be a continuation.”
Yuriy Pyvovarov, then Ukraine’s ambassador to Senegal, shared Yusov’s interview on Facebook, writing, “The work will continue. There will certainly be other results.” Senegal summoned him over the post, while Mali cited the remarks as evidence of Kiev’s involvement, and severed diplomatic ties.
What has been reported about Ukrainian involvement since then?
Le Monde reported in 2024 that Ukrainian intelligence had taught Tuareg rebels to build and operate explosive drones, citing sources close to the group. This month, CNN interviewed Ukrainian personnel who said about 15 specialists were assisting the FLA with unmanned aircraft. One described remotely directing rebel drone missions.
Fousseynou Ouattara, vice president of the defense commission of Mali’s transitional council, told TASS in July that authorities had identified fighters who had received drone training in Ukraine. Malian outlet Bamada also reported that soldiers recovered a drone bearing Ukrainian writing and documents allegedly linked to Ukrainian intelligence during operations against JNIM.
What has Ukraine said?
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has rejected the Sahel states’ terrorism allegations, describing them as “groundless and untrue” and calling Mali’s decision to sever ties “hasty.” In August 2024, it said Bamako had provided no evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Tinzaouaten attack. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency also referred CNN to earlier official remarks when approached for comment on its September report of Ukrainian drone specialists assisting rebels in Mali.
Is Mali alone in making the accusation?
Niger and Burkina Faso have also accused Ukraine of supporting armed groups. The three Alliance of Sahel States (AES) members filed a complaint with the UN Security Council in August 2024.
During a televised interview on Sunday reviewing his four years in office, Burkina Faso’s interim President Ibrahim Traore said he had placed Ukraine on his country’s “map of enemies.” Speaking about what he described as attempts to destabilize Mali and Niger, he warned these were “only the beginning.” He cited Pyvovarov’s comment, saying the diplomat had “clearly stated that they were involved” in supporting armed groups in the Sahel.
What does Moscow say?
Russia backs the Sahel states’ accusations. Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused Kiev of “state terrorism” against countries in the region, citing reports of serving Ukrainian troops joining attacks alongside armed groups. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova previously said Kiev was opening a “second front” against Russia in Africa by supporting militants in countries friendly to Moscow.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko told TASS on July 17 that Ukrainian instructors trained in drone warfare were embedded with Islamist militants in Mali. He also alleged Ukrainian involvement in attacks on Russian interests in Libya and support for paramilitary forces in Sudan, extending Moscow’s accusations beyond the Sahel.
Why have the Sahel states turned to Russia?
Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso ended defense ties with France, accusing it of failing to contain the insurgency and interfering in their affairs. They have strengthened counterterrorism cooperation with Russia.
Nearly 49,000 people have been killed in violence linked to militant Islamist groups in the Sahel since 2022, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies said in August.
Mali and Russia signed a military cooperation agreement in June 2019. Bamako sought Russian private military assistance in 2021. Wagner was replaced by Russia’s Defense Ministry-run Africa Corps in June 2025. The corps operates at African governments’ official request, Lavrov said last month.
At the UN on Monday, Diop said the AES remained open to partnerships respecting its members’ sovereignty. “We do not accept dictates; rather, we seek sincere and healthy cooperation,” he said.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region kill three, including a child, and wound seven
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region kill three, including a child, and wound seven
Russian forces continued to strike Kyiv with drones and various types of missiles. An attack early on September 30 killed two people and injured four in Kyiv, the city administration said.
Russian strikes caused fires in the Sviatoshynskyi, Holosiivskyi, Podilskyi, and Solomianskyi districts, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
A Russian strike killed a child in the Kyiv region. Rescuers found the child’s body while clearing rubble from a private home. Three people — a woman, a man, and a child — were injured.

articles.title: Russian drone explodes in Moldova, day after its opposition moves to suspend its pro-EU president. Analyst says that’s no coincidence
articles.body:
A Russian drone exploded in Moldova on 30 September, detonating near the mast of a civilian mobile operator, TV8 reported. Despite previous such attacks, this one may have another purpose, according to Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military analyst.
Moldova, which borders Ukraine and is not in NATO, has become a regular waypoint and casualty of Russia's drone war, with wreckage turning up repeatedly this year. What sets this strike apart is its timing, days into a fight over the country's pro-EU president.
A drone hits a telecoms mast
Police were alerted at 5:43 a.m. to a drone flying low over Bender, in Transnistria, the general police inspectorate said. It came down near Hîrbovăț and detonated against the mast of a civilian mobile operator, leaving blast marks along about 12 meters of the structure, with the metal deformed and scorched. Service was not disrupted. Police cordoned off the area, and specialists were examining the debris.
A second drone follows
Hours later, at 10:26, Moldova's air-monitoring system detected a second drone crossing its airspace, jet-powered and heading toward the northern town of Soroca, Moldova's Defense Ministry reported, according to European Pravda.
Flights were suspended over the country's north and center. Parliament speaker Igor Grosu condemned the strike: "Russia will answer for its war crimes," he says.
An analyst ties it to the impeachment
Meanwhile, Russian drones entering Moldova on this day is no coincidence, he argues, coming as the opposition moves against President Maia Sandu.
On 29 September, 46 opposition lawmakers registered a motion to suspend her, a step that would need 67 of parliament's 101 votes to pass and, if approved, a referendum within 30 days, Moldova Live reported.
Kovalenko contends pro-Russian forces are running a destabilization campaign they will reinforce with periodic drone attacks, pressing a message at Moldovans: "if you don't want war, get rid of Sandu."

articles.title: Iran to fire as many as missiles if necessary to deter enemy
articles.body:
Speaking in an interview, Brigadier General Ali Balali said missile technology is more complex and challenging than many other methods and weapons, noting that launching a missile is commonly used as an example of a particularly difficult task.
Referring to the products displayed at an exhibition, he said all the equipment on display is domestically developed and manufactured.
“We have made use of the knowledge available around the world and acted in a way that the barriers and sanctions imposed on the country, despite the efforts of those behind them, could not prevent the Islamic Republic of Iran from building up its power and advancing in the missile, drone and other fields,” Balali said.
Balali also outlined the limitations the Islamic Republic faced in its missile capabilities during Iraq’s war of aggression against Iran in the 1980s, saying the country faced severe restrictions in the field at the time.
“During the eight years of the Sacred Defense, we fired a total of 88 missiles,” he said, noting that the weapons were extremely expensive and Iran lacked the resources to fully cover their costs.
“As a result, we had no choice but to launch the missiles one at a time and in limited numbers so that we could sustain operations until the end of the war,” Balali said. “Today, thanks to God, we no longer face such a problem.”
The IRGC Aerospace Force commander’s adviser stressed that Iran’s current defense capabilities allow it to respond powerfully to attacks.
“Today, in every operation, the armed forces launch as much as necessary, with power and determination, so that the enemy is disciplined and understands that the era of ‘hit and run’ is over,” he said.
He added that during the latest aggression, the enemy launched a limited number of strikes, while Iran responded several times over, Press TV reported.
Balali said Iran’s missile production and launch rate is such that the country could sustain operations at the current pace even if a confrontation continued for several years.
He further said that Iranian officials also have comprehensive plans regarding the use of the country’s military capabilities and weapons and act under the guidance and supervision of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei.

articles.title: Seoul suspects Zelenskyy revealed North Korean POW transfer to win arms support
articles.body:
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war.
South Korea's spy agency believes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of two North Korean POWs to boost public support in South Korea for providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy disclosed last week that his country had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, saying they were "not easy to capture alive."
Hours after Zelenskyy's remarks at the United Nations, South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives from any repercussions in North Korea.
On Monday, Seoul summoned Ukraine's envoy in the South to express "serious concerns" over Kyiv's disclosure of the transfer.
Lawmaker Yoo Yeong-ha said on Wednesday that Seoul's spy agency believes Zelenskyy "may have decided to disclose the transfer" in the hope that it could "generate public support in Seoul for providing Ukraine with weapons and other forms of assistance."
Another lawmaker, Youn Kun-young, said the two POWs arrived in South Korea from Ukraine in mid-September.
They were "in generally good health, with no major health concerns," he said, adding the two's "willingness to come to South Korea was confirmed several times," citing Seoul's spy agency.
Earlier this week, Seoul's foreign ministry said that "as the matter concerns the personal safety of the individuals involved and their families," the two sides, Seoul and Kyiv, had "agreed to handle it confidentially."
Lawmaker Yoo said on Wednesday there was no agreement between the South Korean and Ukrainian leaders to keep the matter confidential, but that diplomatic officials from the two sides had agreed to confidentiality during their communications.
"From the outset of the discussions, the Ukrainian side proactively requested strict confidentiality, citing concerns about the potential impact on future prisoner exchanges (with Russia)," he added.
Ukraine captured the two North Korean soldiers early last year among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow.
One of them told South Korean media he was conscripted aged 17 and had served in a reconnaissance unit.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
The row also risks complicating Kyiv's requests to Seoul for armaments supplies.
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war.
Nevertheless, it has been considering requests for defensive weapons, especially since North Korea deployed troops to support Russia in pushing back a surprise Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region in 2024.

articles.title: Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code
articles.body:
A Ukrainian combat simulator can now be found and ordered in NATO's supply catalogs by a single code. L7 Simulators, whose trainers have prepared more than 500,000 Ukrainian troops, has had its entire lineup NATO-codified, with each device assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number, Defender Media reports.
L7's more than 50 trainers, from the Browning M2 to the Stinger to the NLAW, now carry those codes, and the company can codify new ones itself, opening the door to government procurement in Ukraine and across the alliance. It is another Ukrainian defense maker stepping toward NATO's standards and supply chain.
Every trainer gets a NATO number
A NATO Stock Number is a unique 13-digit code, a kind of military barcode for supplies, that lets defense logistics systems across the alliance identify, catalog, and purchase equipment. Every simulator in L7's catalog now has one, and the firm has also won the status to assign numbers to its future products directly, rather than starting the process over for each one.
The code identifies, not certifies
The company is careful about what the step does and does not mean. Codification is not a certification that the product meets NATO's technical standards, L7 stresses, but rather a mechanism for unambiguously identifying an item within the shared defense-logistics system.
The firm entered that system in December 2024, when its UNITS training platform, already cleared for use by Ukraine's Defense Ministry, received the first number.
Half a million have trained on them
L7's range runs to more than 50 types of trainers, tied together in a single ecosystem the company calls UNITS: fire-training systems, anti-tank and air-defense simulators, and trainers for unmanned aircraft, with models for the Stinger, NLAW, Carl Gustaf, RPG-7, and SPG-9 among them.
The simulators are used by the armed forces, the National Guard, and other security agencies, and more than 500,000 service members have trained on them, with over 70,000 of them free of charge at the company's own training center.

articles.title: Estonia prioritizes national defense, postpones Rail Baltica completion in 2027 budget
articles.body:
Estonia’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 with €20.2 billion in expenditure, €19.4 billion in revenue and a projected general government deficit of 4 percent of GDP, ERR reports.
National defence will receive €2.2 billion, keeping defence spending above 5 percent of GDP, with funding for ammunition, drones and stronger air and missile defence capabilities.
The government will continue its agreed 10 percent spending cuts for 2025–2027, while increasing teachers’ pay and funding preparations for nuclear energy.
Business development measures include €134 million for research, development and innovation, alongside more than €30 million earmarked for artificial intelligence and €21 million for cybersecurity.
Rail Baltica will receive €445 million, although the government plans to slow the pace of investment to limit pressure on the budget and construction costs.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone strike injures 12, mostly students, in Russia – governor
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strike injures 12, mostly students, in Russia – governor
Twelve people, most of whom are students, have been injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s Bryansk Region, acting Governor Egor Kovalchuk has said.
The UAV incursion targeted the city of Trubchevsk, sitting on the Desna River in the southern part of the region, not far from the border with Ukraine, Kovalchuk wrote in a post on social media on Wednesday.
“Horrific attack on civilians in Trubchevsk; there are children among the wounded,” he said.
At least seven of those injured were students, with one of the victims being in serious condition, according to the acting governor.
On Monday, Ukrainian drone strikes damaged a railway bridge and tracks at three locations in Bryansk Region, causing several trains to derail.
Part of a bridge collapsed on the Dyatkovo-Lyudinovo rail section, sending ten cars off the tracks, according to Kovalchuk. A separate strike in Unecha District derailed another 18 empty freight cars, A third attack damaged tracks in Navlya District, but did not disrupt train traffic or cause injuries.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately targeting civilians with long-range drones in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
One of the deadliest such strikes came in May when several waves of Ukrainian UAVs hit a student dormitory in the Donbass city of Starobelsk, killing 21 people, mostly young women.
Russia has responded to Kiev’s terrorist attacks by intensifying its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

articles.title: Ukrainian Air Force: 285 attack drones detected over Ukraine on Wed, 254 shot down
articles.body:
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that as of 18:30, 285 enemy strike drones of various types were detected in Ukrainian airspace, and 254 were shot down or neutralized.
"Throughout the day on September 30 (from 06:30 to 18:30), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 285 attack UAVs (174 of which were jet-powered), Gerber drones, and other types of drones," according to a statement by the Ukrainian Air Force on Telegram on Wednesday.
Air defense forces managed to shoot down or neutralize 254 UAVs (146 of them jet-powered).
In addition, according to the Air Force, the enemy launched a strike in the eastern sector using a ballistic missile and several Banderole/Dan-T drones. The information is being verified.
As of 18:30, there were about 10 attack drones in the airspace.
"Do not ignore the air raid alert," the Ukrainian Air Force said in the statement.
